These embeddings serve as enriched input features for downstream fraud models, significantly enhancing their precision (up to 18% relative PR-AUC improvement) by uncovering nuanced behavioral dependencies missed by traditional tabular statistics. The system operates via an hourly batch inference pipeline on Google Cloud, aggregating session histories to produce embeddings that reflect the underlying structure of customer interactions, enabling more robust detection of fraudulent behavior while maintaining scalability for future applications like churn prediction and personalization.

Stitch Fix addresses the challenge of scaling high-quality, brand-aligned text content creation for marketing and e-commerce by deploying an expert-in-the-loop generative AI solution powered by fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). Intended for use by copywriters and marketing teams, their approach combines deep learning techniques—including latent style embeddings and few-shot learning—with human expert review for generating engaging ad headlines and detailed product descriptions that reflect personal style keywords and brand tone. Constraints include maintaining originality, truthful product representation, and alignment with brand guidelines, which are ensured through iterative human oversight. This hybrid system accelerates content production with significant time savings and improved quality compared to purely human or purely algorithmic approaches, fostering a continuous feedback loop that refines generation performance and supports future extensions into styling and personalized textual expression.

Grammarly addressed limitations in text editing by developing CoEdIT, an instruction-tuned large language model (LLM) specialized for text editing tasks, targeting users needing intelligent writing assistance with improved fluency, coherence, clarity, and style. By constructing a dense task-specific dataset from IteraTeR+ with carefully paraphrased natural language editing instructions and fine-tuning pre-trained FLAN-T5 models of varying sizes (770M to 11B parameters), CoEdIT achieves state-of-the-art performance on syntactic, semantic, and stylistic editing benchmarks, outperforming much larger models like GPT3-Edit while being up to 60 times smaller. CoEdIT also generalizes well to adjacent and composite editing tasks, showing superior human-evaluated fluency and accuracy, and is openly available, enabling reproducibility and further development.

Airbnb addressed the challenge of categorizing millions of diverse property listings into thematic categories like "Lakefront" to enhance user browsing by combining machine learning with human-in-the-loop review. The solution leveraged extensive structured and unstructured data sources—including host-provided listing attributes, guest reviews, wishlists, points of interest (POIs) from host guidebooks, Airbnb experiences, and external geospatial data—and applied ML models to extract and integrate these signals for candidate generation. Rule-based heuristics initially generated category candidates scored by confidence metrics weighted by feature importance (e.g., proximity to lake POIs for Lakefront). Human agents then reviewed high-confidence candidates, validating category membership, selecting cover photos, and rating listing quality. Feedback from human reviews enabled the training of dedicated binary XGBoost classification models per category with engineered features such as distances to refined POIs, imaging embeddings, and textual keyword extraction, improving precision and enabling higher automation by progressively promoting listings directly via ML scores. Additional ML models—like a Vision Transformer for optimal cover photo selection and a multi-class classifier for listing quality—further streamlined and scaled the review process. This hybrid approach allowed Airbnb to iteratively improve category accuracy, candidate coverage, and user discovery by continuously refining POI databases, expanding labeled datasets, and planning integration of generative vision and large language models for review tasks.

Lifen addresses the challenge of supporting over 1 million daily NLP model predictions by developing lifen-ai-explainer, a web application designed for Data Scientists and Customer Support to streamline AI support processes through accessible, explainable AI tools. This tool anonymizes documents and AI predictions, providing insights into model decisions, such as highlighting influential words in classification tasks (e.g., patient gender detection) and displaying token-level softmax outputs to debug Named Entity Recognition (NER) models. To enhance interpretability despite constraints like avoiding transformers due to resource limits, they incorporated a global attention layer atop an Embedding + LSTM architecture, yielding attention scores that reveal word importance. Built with a React frontend and FastAPI backend tightly integrated with the main lifen-ai codebase in a mono repo, the system ensures maintainability, synchronization with evolving AI models, and robust type-checked CI workflows. Since mid-2020, this solution has improved trust and error analysis by making the AI’s decision process transparent and maintainable within fast-paced healthcare contexts.

Stripe Radar addresses the challenge of real-time online fraud detection for businesses and consumers by leveraging machine learning to assess over 1,000 transaction features within 100 milliseconds, aiming to accurately distinguish fraudulent from legitimate payments in a dataset where fraud is rare (~0.1%). Intended for Stripe users processing payments, Radar has evolved from simpler models to a sophisticated pure deep neural network (DNN) architecture inspired by ResNeXt, enabling faster training, better scalability, and enhanced feature representation without sacrificing recall. The solution continuously refines features based on detailed fraud pattern analysis and network-wide data, achieving significant accuracy improvements with increased training data. Additionally, Radar emphasizes explainability through risk insights that help users understand and act on fraud decisions, balancing the tradeoff between detection performance and interpretability, ultimately providing businesses with an adaptive, high-precision fraud prevention tool that minimizes false positives and supports confident transactions.

Monzo addresses the challenge of understanding customer saving behaviors from nearly 5 million highly variable, free-text and emoji-rich Pot names—short labels customers use to personalize savings goals—by applying biterm topic modelling, an unsupervised machine learning technique suited for short texts that identifies word co-occurrence patterns to cluster Pots into meaningful thematic topics. Using a cleaned and lemmatized dataset of 800k unique Pot names, including the conversion of emojis to text equivalents, the model was tuned for optimal coherence and yielded 20 distinct topics such as bills, holidays, and life events, supported by over 500 keywords and emojis for classification. This semantic retrieval approach enables Monzo to categorize even one-word Pots via curated keyword lists, uncover seasonal trends in saving habits, and leverage emoji usage to refine insights on customer intent, ultimately equipping product teams with nuanced behavioral understanding to tailor features that better meet diverse customer saving goals.

Dropbox faces the business challenge of quickly and accurately evaluating A/B experiments for subscription-based products, where user satisfaction and revenue manifest over extended periods rather than immediate engagements like ad clicks. The intended users are data scientists and product teams aiming to optimize product onboarding and subscription conversions. Their solution leverages a machine learning model predicting eXpected Revenue (XR), a personalized metric calculated within days of trial start that forecasts a user's two-year lifetime value by modeling conversion probability, retention, and plan changes. Using Gradient Boosted Trees and calibrated with historical data segmented by trial type and geography, XR enables statistically sensitive and accelerated experimental conclusions with approximately 3% systematic uncertainty, overcoming limitations of traditional short-term KPIs like 7-day activity or 90-day retention metrics. XR computations are integrated into a data pipeline utilizing TensorFlow, Spark, Hive, and AWS infrastructure, supporting not only rapid experiment analysis but also ongoing business health monitoring and product customization insights, ultimately allowing Dropbox to run more frequent experiments with higher confidence in subscriber satisfaction and revenue impact.

Dropbox addressed the challenge of tedious file organization, especially for team administrators responsible for managing large volumes of files, by developing "smart move," an AI-assisted feature released in 2021 that leverages machine learning to analyze a user’s existing folder structures and suggest appropriate subfolders for unsorted files. Recognizing organization as a highly personal task, the solution employs a human-in-the-loop workflow allowing users to review, accept, or reject suggestions, ensuring user control and trust. The core ML model was trained using millions of internally sourced examples of well-organized folders, encoding file and folder names with embeddings that capture semantic and file-type similarity, then scoring candidate folders for file placement via a deep neural network. Key constraints included strict privacy measures on filenames, synchronous low-latency suggestions to maintain a smooth UX, and adapting to diverse organizational patterns. Internal testing showed the trained model outperformed simple heuristics in accuracy (73% vs. 64%), but in external alpha tests, heuristic suggestions slightly outperformed the model in user acceptance, highlighting the importance of user perception alongside accuracy. Smart move significantly reduced manual file management effort while keeping users in control and served as a reusable model for related Dropbox features, with ongoing exploration into alternative workflows and large language model applications to further enhance semantic retrieval and file organization.

Roblox addresses the resource-intensive challenge of joining large fact and unpartitioned dimension tables in its petabyte-scale data lake by employing Learned Bloom Filters—ML-optimized data structures that predict key presence to pre-filter dimension data before joins. Facing constraints like biased training data with sparse overlap between fact and dimension keys, non-informative unique identifiers, and the need for low-latency inference, Roblox implemented a Sandwich Learned Bloom Filter approach integrating traditional Bloom Filters to rebalance datasets and gradient-boosted trees leveraging dimension attributes for accurate predictions. This solution significantly reduces Bloom Filter size by 17-42%, trims shuffled data volume by approximately 80%, lowers CPU usage by up to 60%, and stabilizes query runtimes, resulting in an average 25% daily cost saving across multiple production workloads while enhancing operational reliability.

Wayfair addresses the challenge of rapidly identifying high-potential new products amid a vast, expanding catalog and the cold start problem by deploying the Predicted Winners suite of machine learning models, intended for product managers and business teams to prioritize marketing and merchandising investments efficiently. The core solution consists of the Day Zero model, which uses intrinsic product features—such as wholesale costs, images, and descriptions processed through deep learning embeddings—to predict long-term sales potential at launch, integrated with storefront sorting for product visibility, and the Continuous Winners model, which refines predictions over time by analyzing multivariate customer engagement time series (visits, add-to-carts, orders) using LSTM networks to automatically extract salient temporal features. To mitigate bias from promotional exposure, the Sentinel testing framework ensures model predictions reflect true product potential independent of investment effects. The architecture employs knowledge sharing across product categories to improve predictions for less-populated classes and new product types with scarce data, enhanced by training objectives optimized to reflect the real statistical characteristics of revenue and order data, including uncertainty quantification for risk management. The expected outcome is accelerated success and better investment efficiency for new products, driving improved customer experience through earlier access to high-quality, relevant offerings.

Dropbox's Security team addressed the business problem of prompt injection attacks where user-controlled inputs with control characters, such as backspace ("\b") and carriage-return ("\r"), manipulate large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI's GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 to bypass prompt constraints and induce hallucinations or unintended responses, compromising secure and truthful query answers. Intended users are engineers developing LLM-powered applications requiring robust prompt controls to ensure outputs are confined to provided contexts, avoiding data leaks or misinformation. Through experiments injecting thousands of encoded control characters into prompt templates, Dropbox demonstrated how these inputs cause LLMs to "forget" instructions or context and hallucinate answers, a behavior undocumented in model references and challenging in prompt engineering. Important data include prompt templates enforcing context-bound truthful Q&A and the complex encoding of control sequences in JSON payloads. The expected outcome is to inform the community on the novel control character prompt injection technique, guiding future development of input sanitization and secure prompt engineering strategies to mitigate abuse while balancing valid use cases that require control character handling.

Airbnb addresses the challenge of incomplete or inconsistent listing attribute data—critical for matching guest needs such as workspace availability or child-friendly amenities—by developing the Listing Attribute Extraction Platform (LAEP), an AI-driven semantic retrieval system that processes anonymized, unstructured text from multiple sources to automatically extract structured information. LAEP incorporates a custom Named Entity Recognition model trained on labeled domain-specific data to identify entities like amenities, hospitality features, and points of interest; an Entity Mapping module that uses word embeddings and cosine similarity to normalize diverse textual expressions into Airbnb’s standardized attribute taxonomy; and an Entity Scoring component leveraging a fine-tuned BERT classifier to determine attribute presence with confidence scores. This end-to-end ML/NLP pipeline enriches Airbnb’s listing knowledge base, powering downstream applications like the Attribute Prioritization System and enhancing personalized guest experiences by scaling accurate attribute extraction while preserving privacy through anonymization and classification design.

Snap's Spotlight platform addresses the challenge of real-time personalized short-video recommendations from a massive content pool with limited textual metadata by employing an embedding-based retrieval system using scalable two-tower models. These models separately generate dense user and story embeddings from diverse, independent sparse and dense features including user demographics, past engagement, creator data, and content embeddings, ensuring user privacy by isolating individual user data. Using a ResNet-style neural architecture and optimized training with Adam optimizer, cosine annealing, and in-batch negative sampling, the system produces 128-dimensional embeddings that maximize retrieval recall via approximate nearest neighbor search with HNSW indexing. Offline embedding generation pipelines update the user and story representations at different cadences, feeding into a scalable serving infrastructure that separates feed processing and retrieval services to manage diverse query loads efficiently. This approach, integrating multiple engagement signals and additional retrieval sources, has led to significant improvements in user engagement metrics on Spotlight, with ongoing plans to leverage transformer models for richer user sequence encoding and unify EBR techniques for further efficiency and personalization.

Airbnb addresses the business problem of understanding guest preferences for home attributes to better match guests with suitable Hosts by analyzing unstructured text data from messages, reviews, and customer support tickets using a machine learning system called Attribute Prioritization System (APS). The system employs LATEX, which combines a named entity recognition (NER) model based on textCNN to extract key phrases and an unsupervised entity mapping module leveraging word embeddings to map these phrases to specific home attributes, enabling scalable, language-agnostic extraction of guest interests like amenities and location features. Users include Airbnb Hosts, who receive personalized recommendations on which amenities to acquire, highlight, or clarify based on predicted guest interest influenced by home characteristics such as location, property type, capacity, and price, and the system addresses constraints like sparse data in niche home segments by using an inference model to estimate attribute importance across fine-grained categories. The expected outcome is enhanced personalization in listing descriptions and Host advice that helps guests find ideal vacation homes efficiently, thereby improving guest satisfaction and Host performance.

Airbnb addresses the business problem of improving search result diversity to better represent the heterogeneous preferences of their diverse guest population, beyond the conventional Majority principle that ranks listings based on highest booking probability tied to majority preferences such as low price. Intended users are guests searching for listings whose varied preferences include both economical and high-quality options. The proposed solution enhances their existing neural network ranking system with a companion neural network that estimates inter-listing similarity and penalizes listings too similar to those already ranked higher, enabling a more diverse set of search results that balance booking probability with listing dissimilarity. Training data leverages historical logged search results and booking behavior, ensuring the algorithm captures guest preference heterogeneity and avoids redundant listing choices. Expected outcomes include increased uncancelled bookings (+0.29%), higher booking value (+0.8%) indicative of better quality listings, and improved guest satisfaction reflected by a 0.4% rise in 5-star ratings, demonstrating the success of incorporating diversity through semantic similarity estimation in ranking.

Picnic addresses the business challenge of accurately forecasting grocery demand to minimize food waste and ensure customer satisfaction by employing scalable, deep learning-based machine learning models such as Temporal Fusion Transformers, leveraging extensive contextual data including product details, holidays, weather, promotions, and recipes stored in a Snowflake data warehouse. Intended users include operations teams relying on precise purchase order predictions for thousands of products across multiple warehouses. The solution involves continuous automated retraining and rigorous validation with tools like Pandera for data quality and outlier detection, supported by GPU-enabled infrastructure to manage data and concept drift while pre-computing vast quantities of predictions to ensure low-latency, robust delivery to operational systems. This approach balances advanced ML techniques with software engineering best practices to achieve scalable, reliable forecasting capable of adapting to changes and preventing disruption from model errors, ultimately optimizing supply chain efficiency and sustainability.

The business problem addresses identifying semantically similar products across competing e-commerce inventories to inform pricing strategies, detect assortment gaps, and find duplicates within one’s own product range. Intended users include retail and assortment analysts requiring efficient and accurate product matching. The proposed solution first applies Lexical Matching based on word overlap with efficiency via inverted indices but limited by exact word matching; then leverages a Semantic Encoder (fine-tuned SBERT) to capture deeper contextual meaning beyond lexical similarity; finally, a two-stage Retrieval-Rerank method uses fast lexical retrieval to generate candidate matches followed by a transformer-based cross-encoder to rerank pairs for higher precision. The system employs hard negative sampling to train models on difficult non-matching but semantically close examples, maximizing discriminative accuracy. Constraints involve processing unordered sets of product titles, handling variations like synonyms, misspellings, or missing words, and balancing scalability with accuracy. The expected outcome is a robust, scalable semantic product matching framework that improves assortment diversity and competitive insight by accurately linking equivalent or similar products despite lexical variations.

The business problem involves enabling users of Honeycomb's observability platform to query complex instrumentation data using natural language, aiming to simplify data retrieval for engineers and analysts who may not be proficient in Honeycomb’s query syntax. The proposed solution is the Query Assistant, an LLM-driven natural language interface that translates user inputs into Honeycomb’s query language, incorporating domain-specific schema, query structure, and contextual instrumentation details into prompt engineering. Key constraints include the limited LLM context window impacting the handling of schemas with thousands of fields, slow and latency-prone LLM responses that preclude chaining calls, challenges in prompt engineering to balance correctness with usefulness for broad or ambiguous inputs, and significant risks of prompt injection necessitating non-destructive query execution and strict output validation. Additional constraints arise from legal and compliance requirements for data privacy and customer contractual obligations, requiring security audits and tailored terms of service. The expected outcome is a best-effort, user-refinable query generation that is not perfect but practical, emphasizing that LLMs serve as engines for features rather than standalone products, and that real-world deployment demands extensive design iteration, user feedback, and operational safeguards.

GitHub faced the business problem of improving developer productivity through code generation, aiming to provide users—primarily software developers—with intelligent coding assistance within their IDEs. Leveraging OpenAI’s evolving large language models (LLMs), starting from GPT-3 and progressing to the specialized multilingual Codex model trained on billions of lines of public code, GitHub developed Copilot to offer context-aware, interactive code completions and suggestions. Critical data considerations included the integration of contextual cues such as neighboring editor tabs and file path information to improve model prompt crafting and fine-tuning, ensuring relevant, language-specific, and accurate code outputs. Constraints involved handling vast model complexity, interpreting user acceptance or rejection of suggestions without typical engineering diagnostics, and adapting the model effectively across diverse programming languages and projects. The expected outcome was a substantially enhanced developer experience, with higher acceptance rates of AI-generated code, enabling users to code more efficiently by automating routine lookup and code synthesis tasks within the development environment.

The Personal Voice use case addresses the challenge faced by individuals at risk of losing their natural speech, such as those diagnosed with ALS, by enabling them to create a synthesized voice that resembles their own for communication across calls, FaceTime, and assistive apps. Users record 150 sentences on their Apple device, and a machine learning pipeline—comprising a pretrained then fine-tuned FastSpeech2-based acoustic model and WaveRNN vocoder—is executed entirely on-device to preserve privacy and enable offline use. Fine-tuning both acoustic and vocoder models using on-device training improves voice quality and speaker similarity, while an on-device speech recording enhancement pipeline employing noise filtering, voice isolation, U-Net mel spectrum augmentation, and CarGAN audio recovery models helps mitigate real-world noise contamination in recordings, further enhancing output fidelity. The system leverages a large, diverse speaker dataset (LibriTTS) for pretraining and optimizes for low latency and memory efficiency, delivering a personalized text-to-speech solution that optimizes model size and inference speed, thereby providing ALS patients and similar users an accessible, private, and high-quality tool to maintain their vocal identity and participate in conversations through real-time synthesized speech.

Stitch Fix faced the business challenge of debugging and improving its complex, modular personalized search pipeline, which serves clients discovering tailored fashion styles via the Freestyle feature. Intended users include data scientists, engineers, UX researchers, designers, and product managers working collaboratively to iterate on search quality and relevance. The proposed solution, Ariadne, is a custom React-based observability UI that visualizes the entire search pipeline—from query parsing through ElasticSearch core ranking to personalized reranking—using interactive Sankey diagrams, linked multi-view result displays, and detailed metric plots. Ariadne enables pinpointing which service or pipeline stage causes anomalies, tracking specific items’ journeys, and conducting “what if” analyses by modifying queries, pipeline configurations, and client profiles to anticipate and resolve issues before user impact. This approach relies on rich logging and metrics across named entity recognition, ranking, and personalization components, addressing the constraints of rapid experimentation and complex service dependencies. The expected outcome is accelerated development, clearer diagnosis of search failures, enhanced collaboration, and improved personalized search relevance for end clients.

Microsoft 365 Systems Innovation research addresses the challenge of efficiently diagnosing and mitigating cloud incidents affecting large-scale hyperscale services by leveraging large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and GPT-3.5. Intended for incident management engineers, the solution automatically generates root cause analyses and mitigation recommendations from incident tickets containing titles and summaries, using semantic retrieval and fine-tuned LLMs evaluated on over 40,000 real production incidents across 1,000+ services. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 models significantly outperform earlier versions, improving lexical similarity scores by over 45% for root cause and 130% for mitigation generation and demonstrating usefulness in real-time settings as rated by engineers. Constraints include handling diverse incident types, maintaining model freshness amidst evolving data, and integrating contextual signals like logs and service metrics. The expected outcome is accelerated, more accurate incident resolution, reducing human effort and improving cloud service reliability and customer satisfaction through AI-powered automated incident management.

LinkedIn addressed the challenge of improving subscription renewal payment success by replacing a complex, static rule-based payment gateway routing system with an adaptive machine-learning-driven engine. Targeting LinkedIn members and customers subscribing to Premium and Sales Navigator products, the ML solution framed payment routing as a supervised learning problem to predict the optimal payment gateway based on transaction features such as card type, transaction type, and product family. To handle sample imbalance from prior routing rules, inverse probability weighting (IPW) was employed during bootstrap sampling to generate unbiased training data. A multiclass softmax logistic regression model was trained on US transaction data to forecast gateway success probabilities, improving routing decisions dynamically. Deployed via A/B testing, the model achieved statistically significant increases in payment approval rates, reducing involuntary subscription suspensions and cancellations due to avoidable payment failures. The solution incorporates continuous model refreshes and anticipates future enhancements including expanded geographical features and alternative ML approaches such as multi-armed bandits for non-stationary environments.

Yelp addresses the challenge of efficiently tagging, organizing, and ranking vast amounts of user-generated content such as reviews, business metadata, and photos to enhance content accessibility and quality for users. Targeting internal machine learning teams and ultimately consumers, Yelp employs semantic embeddings generated via models like the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) for text and OpenAI's CLIP for images to create low-dimensional vector representations capturing business context, sentiment, and visual semantics. Despite fine-tuning attempts on Yelp-specific data for USE, the off-the-shelf model proved equally effective across diverse NLP tasks including categorization, sentiment analysis, and relevance ranking. Business embeddings are constructed by averaging recent review embeddings and aim to support recommendations through similarity measures. CLIP's zero-shot capabilities enable semantic photo classification without extensive labeled data, showing promising results compared to domain-trained ResNet50 models, though label engineering and threshold tuning are needed to mitigate misclassifications influenced by photo composition and typographic confounders. Yelp now maintains a comprehensive database of hundreds of millions of vector embeddings facilitating improved search, recommendation, and content analysis functions across the platform.

Expedia Group addresses the challenge of efficiently recommending relevant travel products from a massive item corpus by implementing a two-stage recommendation system, targeting data scientists and ML engineers working on recommender systems. The solution uses a two-tower neural network architecture—composed of separate user (query) and item encoders—to generate candidate items from large datasets of traveler interactions and property features, such as location and amenities, extracted from anonymized search impression data. By employing in-batch sampled SoftMax loss with critical logQ correction to mitigate popularity bias, and leveraging PySpark for data preprocessing and TensorFlow Recommenders for model training, this approach enables scalable candidate retrieval followed by reranking. The expected outcome is improved recall@k in retrieving relevant travel options, optimized through approximate nearest neighbor search (e.g., SCANN) and validated with real Expedia traveler data.

Shopify faces the challenge of measuring app quality improvement when it's impractical to audit every app daily, necessitating reliance on a sampled success metric—the "shop issue rate," representing average app requirement violations detected through monthly random audits. To discern real trends from sampling noise, Shopify employs Monte Carlo simulations that generate synthetic audit data by sampling from a Poisson distribution, reflecting the count of issues per app, while varying parameters such as sample size and expected monthly improvement rates. These simulations compute variability metrics like mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the probability of observing decreases over time (e.g., 1-month decreases observed), enabling the evaluation of how many apps must be audited to confidently detect quality changes attributable to review processes. The approach provides stakeholders with quantifiable trade-offs between audit cost and metric certainty, guiding resource allocation for app quality assessment under uncertainty.

Honeycomb addressed the challenge of easing the steep learning curve in querying observability data by building Query Assistant, an AI-powered feature leveraging large language models (LLMs) to translate natural language inputs into Honeycomb's query DSL. Targeting new and existing users—especially those unfamiliar with complex query construction—the solution aimed to accelerate product activation by facilitating natural language querying and encouraging transition to manual, complex queries, board creation, and alert triggers. Key usage and activation metrics indicated strong correlations: teams using Query Assistant showed higher query retention, more creation of complex queries and Boards, and improved engagement, though adoption varied by pricing tier and did not fully drive alert-trigger creation. Operational constraints included managing prompt size, latency, and model choice to control costs, resulting in minimal monthly expenses (~$30) using GPT-3.5-turbo and text-embedding-ada-002. Emergent user behaviors—such as entering domain-specific scripting or trace IDs—highlighted unforeseen but productive LLM interpretation. Overall, Query Assistant proved a valuable, low-cost augmentation to Honeycomb’s platform, enhancing user onboarding and query proficiency without replacing manual querying, while demonstrating the practical complexities of integrating nondeterministic LLMs into mission-critical SaaS features.

Instacart faced operational complexity and limited user interaction data sharing across multiple browse ad surfaces, each initially supported by separate XGBoost pCTR models with constrained feature incorporation and outdated infrastructure. To address this, they developed a Unified Browse pCTR model using a Deep Learning Wide-and-Deep architecture that consolidates diverse training data from all surfaces into a richer dataset, enabling cross-surface user behavior insights and handling high-cardinality features (e.g., user/product IDs, search terms) via embeddings. Featuring a second-order interaction layer through factorization machines, the model captures complex contextual relationships and missing data patterns effectively. This unified model significantly improved offline metrics and online performance (e.g., up to 190% AUC-PR gain on some surfaces), enhanced ad relevance and return on ad spend (ROAS), increased incremental sales and cart additions, and reduced system latency and maintenance overhead, benefiting Instacart customers, advertisers, and operational teams alike.

This use case addresses demand forecasting in the online fashion industry, targeting data scientists and business analysts facing challenges such as large data volumes, catalog irregularity, high turnover, and fixed inventory constraints. The proposed solution utilizes deep learning models tailored to the domain, specifically adjusting for the fixed inventory assumption by closely modeling the price-demand relationship. The approach leverages historical demand and pricing data to improve forecast accuracy despite irregular product availability. Expected outcomes include enhanced demand predictability, enabling better inventory and pricing decisions in a fast-moving, data-rich e-commerce environment.

The Guardian, collaborating with UCL PhD students, addressed the business problem of accurately attributing quotes in journalistic texts by employing machine learning-based coreference resolution, which links ambiguous anaphoric mentions (e.g., pronouns) to their clear antecedents (the original entities) across complex, multi-sentence contexts. Intended for journalists and data scientists, the solution involved fine-tuning pretrained language models with manually labeled Guardian articles to capture the semantic nuances necessary for precise quote-source matching, overcoming challenges posed by ambiguous references and the subtleties of language such as those tested by the Winograd Schema. This approach leverages word embeddings to represent contextual meaning numerically, enabling the automated identification of who said what with higher precision, thus enriching the Guardian’s archive with reliably attributed quotes to support accurate reporting, fact-checking, and demographic analysis of public opinion.

Wayfair addresses the business problem of delivering accurate promised delivery dates to enhance customer satisfaction and increase sales, especially balancing speed and reliability in supply chain deliveries. The intended users are customers viewing product pages who benefit from precise delivery date predictions. The solution employs a machine-learning model, specifically gradient boosted decision trees via CatBoost, trained end-to-end to predict delivery times from order placement to delivery, replacing the previous segmented approach. Key features include supplier-specific recent shipment times, physical distance between supplier warehouses and customers, temporal order information, and supply chain constraints such as holidays and carrier schedules. Constraints involve extremely low-latency inference to serve tens of millions of daily product views with millisecond response times, requiring high optimization of feature lookups and computation. The outcome is halving the gap between promised and actual delivery times without sacrificing reliability, leading to higher conversion rates and revenue, while the solution remains extendable to other markets and order types with potential future improvements using advanced ML architectures like transformers.

Monzo faced the business problem of optimising marketing messages to promote diverse financial products without overwhelming users, aiming to enhance campaign effectiveness and user experience. Intended users were Monzo’s customers segmented by their differentiated responses to marketing interventions. The solution involved building uplift models using A/B test data to predict the incremental response of users (e.g., increased savings or subscriptions) to specific marketing campaigns. These models classified users into treatment-only, adverse effect, sure things, and never responders, enabling multi-objective optimisation to assign the most relevant product messages while respecting communication constraints. Constraints included internal messaging limits and prioritisation parameters (t) to balance campaigns across products. The expected outcome was a substantial improvement in campaign effectiveness—up to 200%—by targeting users most likely to respond positively, validated through controlled experiments comparing traditional random targeting to the uplift-based approach.

Foodpanda addresses the business problem of maximizing user conversion rates by optimizing the order in which menu categories and products are presented for each vendor across multiple countries through A/B testing, targeting platform users and data engineers. The proposed solution involves scheduling and automating updates of "B versions" of menus via BigQuery tables and an internal API, orchestrated using Apache Airflow DAGs that handle payload generation and API calls. Initial constraints included long run times (9 hours for 5 countries), high failure rates (~4%) due to vendors modifying menus during processing, and inability to scale beyond 14 countries without delays. To overcome these, Foodpanda optimized concurrency by paginating data, creating parallel DAG tasks, prioritizing countries by vendor count, using dedicated Airflow pools, and allocating more CPUs, which cut processing time by over half (to 3 hours 45 minutes) and lowered failure rates to 2.2%. Expected outcomes include faster, scalable, and more reliable menu ranking experiments that improve A/B test quality and facilitate future dynamic, batch, and country-specific experimentation enhancements.

Wayfair addresses the business challenge of identifying business-to-business (B2B) shoppers who unknowingly browse the consumer site without enrolling in Wayfair Professional, their B2B platform catering to clients like office managers and hotel chains. The intended users are Wayfair’s sales and marketing teams tasked with engaging potential business customers promptly after purchase. The solution, called Hamlet Order Confirmation (OC), is a real-time machine learning model leveraging over 100 features including real-time browsing behavior, order data, marketing interactions, and third-party firmographic data, to predict the likelihood that an order is business-related. Key challenges include creating accurate labels despite incomplete ground truth by combining known customer data, record linkage algorithms matching customers to businesses, and synthetic labels using neural networks, and engineering a low-latency inference pipeline that blends streaming and precomputed features stored in a Vertex feature store and retrieved via Aerospike to meet sub-second SLAs. The approach uses xgboost models optimized for precision-recall AUC to handle class imbalance, with threshold tuning tailored to engagement modalities—favoring high precision for sales calls and high recall for onsite messaging. The expected outcome is enhanced identification of B2B customers immediately following purchase, enabling targeted outreach that doubles the effectiveness of prior heuristic methods, thereby driving increased enrollment in Wayfair Professional and supporting efficient, cost-effective business furnishing solutions.

Spotify faced the business challenge of efficiently managing and scaling paid content marketing campaigns globally to maximize user acquisition and optimize cost per registration (CPR), targeting marketers handling tens of thousands of ads across diverse platforms like Facebook, Google, and TikTok. The intended users were marketing teams needing scalable, localized, and engaging creative assets that reflect Spotify’s content and brand values. To address this, Spotify developed an automated content generation and ad deployment system combining rich metadata from its extensive artist catalog with machine learning-based content ranking models. Initially using Java templating for static ads, they evolved to harness Adobe After Effects via the open-source nexrender system for scalable, animated creative generation across multiple ad formats and languages. They built daily data pipelines ingesting performance metrics and artist popularity, integrating these into a gradient-boosted XGBoost model to predict an artist’s contribution to user registrations and optimize the cost-effectiveness of ads per campaign and region. This ML-driven ranking replaced earlier heuristics, improving click-through and reducing CPR by up to 14%. The system faced constraints including dependency on third-party ad platform APIs, adjustments post-iOS IDFA changes, tooling migrations, and the complexity of encoding artist diversity in recommendations, addressed through robust fallback mechanisms and iterative ML development. The expected outcome was a continuously improving, scalable marketing pipeline that increased monthly active users by 9% and reduced user acquisition costs, uniquely combining Spotify’s content data, creative automation, and predictive analytics to pioneer global automated performance marketing.

Spotify faced the business problem of optimizing in-app messaging, which can variably affect user engagement and retention. The intended users are Spotify listeners, some of whom respond positively to promotional messages while others do not, posing a challenge due to heterogeneous treatment effects. To address this, Spotify employed uplift modeling—a causal inference technique—to predict the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) of sending in-app messages using user features and randomized holdout data. Their multi-output machine learning model, inspired by S-learner, T-learner, and Dragonnet architectures, predicts uplift across multiple business metrics simultaneously, enabling targeted messaging only to users likely to benefit. Offline policy evaluation and A/B testing confirmed that this selective approach improves user retention without harming other key metrics. The solution integrates causal inference with multi-task learning to balance diverse messaging impacts, enabling adaptive, data-driven communication strategies that enhance both user experience and business outcomes.

Instacart faced a complex business problem during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent crises: accurately predicting the availability of millions of grocery items across 80,000+ retail locations to fulfill customer orders efficiently. The intended users include customers relying on real-time product availability, Instacart shoppers who pick items in stores, and retailers integrated into the platform. The proposed solution leverages machine learning models to estimate the probability of item availability, balancing the trade-off between item selection shown to customers and the found rate of ordered items to maintain customer confidence and retention. Constraints include rapidly fluctuating inventory due to supply chain disruptions, diverse inventory management systems among retailers, and the inability to reserve items until picked. Instacart innovated with dynamic thresholds to adapt quickly without retraining models, real-time signals from shoppers’ found/not-found data, and user experience features like “low stock” badges and “Request” buttons to manage customer expectations. The expected outcome is higher order fulfillment rates, improved shopper efficiency, increased customer retention—especially among new customers—and scalable solutions adaptable to future supply volatility.

LinkedIn addresses the business problem of enhancing homepage feed relevance to better engage members by deeply understanding their goals and preferences. The intended users are LinkedIn members seeking personalized professional content. The proposed solution integrates large-scale sparse ID embeddings—such as member, hashtag, and post IDs—into a mixed-effect ranking model, leveraging embedding lookup tables with hundreds of millions of parameters trained on multi-billion records to represent high-dimensional categorical features in a dense vector space. This approach captures member-content interaction patterns, mitigates cold start challenges for new items or users, and enriches personalization by aggregating embeddings of past interactions. To handle significant data volume and model complexity, LinkedIn optimized training through distributed Horovod-based GPU parallelism and efficient data pipeline strategies, and addressed serving scalability by transitioning from external key-value stores to in-memory hosting enabled by enhanced infrastructure and collision-free minimal perfect hashing. This comprehensive methodology achieves a 500x model size scale-up and delivers enhanced recommendation quality, reduced latency, and operational efficiency, ultimately improving member engagement and satisfaction with the feed.

Grab faced the challenge of managing and protecting vast, rapidly growing data entities comprising schemas like database tables and message streams, with a critical need to accurately classify sensitive information, especially Personal Identifiable Information (PII), for fine-grained, table-level access control under internal governance policies. Manual classification was untenable due to scale, inconsistent interpretations by data producers, and inefficiencies. To address this, Grab’s Caspian and Data Governance teams developed an orchestration service named Gemini that integrates large language models (LLMs) like GPT-3.5 alongside third-party classification tools to automatically generate metadata tags at the column level via natural language prompts crafted for precise semantic classification aligned with governance taxonomies. The system batches requests, manages rate limits, and outputs structured JSON tag assignments for columns, enabling downstream verification and iterative improvements. Post-deployment, Gemini achieved high accuracy with minimal manual corrections, scanning over 20,000 data entities rapidly and saving approximately 360 man-days per year while enabling attribute-based access control and dynamic data masking in line with sensitivity tiers. The solution’s prompt engineering, contextual token management, and confidence estimation innovations facilitate scalable, cost-effective metadata generation integral for secure data discovery and compliance across Grab’s ecosystem.

The New York Times Cooking team addresses the challenge of helping users find personalized recipes amid a vast catalog by combining editorial curation with machine-learning-driven recommendations. Intended for app and website users with diverse preferences including diet, nutrition, seasonality, and cuisine, their solution uses text embeddings from recipe titles, descriptions, ingredients, and steps to measure similarity via cosine similarity, enabling features like "Similar Recipes." They employ contextual multi-armed bandit algorithms that balance exploration and exploitation to optimize engagement, incorporating user-specific features derived from saved recipes to tailor recommendations. Additional factors such as seasonal ingredient scores and implicit dietary signals extracted from user interactions (e.g., saved vegetarian or gluten-free recipes) further refine personalization. This multi-faceted approach enhances user experience by dynamically presenting recipes that align with individual tastes and contextual factors, resulting in increased engagement and satisfaction.

DoorDash addresses the challenge of forecasting supply and demand during holidays—periods characterized by high variability and limited data—by adopting a cascade machine learning approach tailored for time-series data. Conventional tree-based models like gradient boosting machines struggle with holiday anomalies due to their inability to capture rare extreme events accurately, leading to systematic over- or under-forecasting. To overcome this, DoorDash first calculates holiday multipliers via thousands of linear regressions that estimate holiday-specific impacts at granular starting point-daypart pairs, then preprocesses input time series to remove holiday effects, trains GBM models on this "holiday-free" data, and finally applies the multipliers post-forecast to adjust predictions. This cascade design retains recent historical information and improves accuracy significantly—reducing weighted mean absolute percentage error (wMAPE) by about 10% averaged over holidays—thus enhancing the proactive mobilization system used by operations, finance, and engineering teams to optimize Dasher allocation and incentive pay. Though experimental evaluations faced power limitations due to network effects and the infrequency of holidays, backtesting and A/B tests on select events showed the approach maintains or improves quality without adverse outcomes, facilitating stakeholder buy-in. While the cascade method adds complexity through additional modeling and preprocessing steps, it offers a scalable, interpretable, and automated forecasting solution that mitigates traditional ML limitations around rare, high-impact events in a richly granular, multi-market context.

DoorDash addressed the challenge of balancing forecasting accuracy, speed, and computational cost for their large-scale, high-dimensional demand forecasting by developing ELITE, an ensemble learning framework for time series estimation that integrates multiple base learners using temporal stacking with a k-fold cross-validation strategy. Targeted at data scientists and operations planners, ELITE replaces exhaustive grid search over single models with a two-layer ensemble architecture parallelized on Ray clusters, yielding up to 95% cost reduction and 78% faster execution while improving accuracy by approximately 10-12%, especially in granular forecasting tasks like switchback-level delivery time variance reduction. This modular system supports diverse model types and incorporates external factors such as holidays and promotions, enhancing stability and reducing maintenance complexity by minimizing repeated base model training. Although ensemble performance may degrade in extreme, specialized scenarios, ELITE generally improves forecast robustness and efficiency in real-world volatile time series, enabling scalable, automated forecasting across thousands of targets within practical resource constraints.

Delivery Hero addresses the challenge of retaining customers and enhancing their delivery experience by developing personalized recommendation models based on semantic retrieval of customer preferences. Intended for data scientists and machine learning engineers, the solution leverages both explicit feedback, such as direct ratings, and implicit feedback derived from app interactions like order frequency, vendor engagement, and food type preferences, to build detailed customer profiles. To overcome the sparsity of explicit data, the system applies similarity metrics like cosine similarity on feature vectors (incorporating factors such as order count and dietary preferences) to identify similar customers and generate vendor recommendation scores accordingly, while carefully respecting dietary constraints to avoid negative experiences. To scale these recommendations across millions of customers and thousands of vendors, Delivery Hero employs collaborative filtering with matrix factorization, producing embeddings that represent customers and vendors for efficient scoring and further integration into machine learning pipelines. The expected outcome is an interpretable and scalable personalized vendor recommendation system that continuously improves through ongoing model refinement and comprehensive evaluation.

Delivery Hero addresses the cold start problem for new app users by developing a personalized restaurant ranking system that enhances initial user retention and engagement. Since collaborative filtering is ineffective without prior user interactions, they employ a content-based filtering approach relying on key features such as cuisine, budget, delivery time, fees, location, and popularity approximated by distance. Starting with a simple baseline model optimized via Bayesian search to maximize NDCG ranking performance, they further improve the system using LambdaMART, a learning-to-rank algorithm combining LambdaRank and gradient-boosted trees, incorporating additional features like short-term popularity and preparation time. This machine-learning-driven solution enables new customers to efficiently discover relevant restaurants, improving user experience and platform stickiness.

The system integrates backend services with scalable data storage and Spark-based prediction jobs. Since its 2021 launch, Bullseye has demonstrably increased sales, improved budget utilization, and reduced promo spend across categories like food and Mart campaigns, enabling Grab to scale targeted, intelligent marketing efforts that better align promos with merchant business goals.

Grab addressed the challenge of efficiently reaching target audiences in its scalable advertising platform, focusing on advertisers seeking to expand lookalike audiences—groups resembling existing customers—to enhance campaign effectiveness. Previous systems suffered from long audience creation SLAs (up to two days), high costs, low scalability, outdated audience updates (weekly), and unstable data ingestion. The solution uses semantic retrieval via embeddings—compressed vector representations of users and audiences—to enable real-time, in-memory retrieval of the top N lookalike audiences per user, leveraging passenger and audience embeddings with cosine similarity thresholds. A passenger embedding compression technique based on hash functions reduces memory use by about 90%, allowing storage of 20GB of user embeddings without latency penalties. Audiences are created by averaging passenger embeddings connected to campaign metadata, updated with a low-cost neural network, and served instantly—reducing creation time to minutes, doubling impressions and clicks, improving CTR, conversion rates, ROI, and cutting generation costs by 98%. This pipeline supports millions of users and dynamically adapts to representation drift among entities, optimizing for both accuracy and cost, making the system robust for fast, scalable targeted advertising in a complex, data-intensive environment.

BlaBlaCar addressed the business problem of phishing and fraud perpetrated by scammers creating fake profiles and trips to illicitly obtain payment information from users. Targeting platform members vulnerable to social engineering, the fraud detection team comprised engineers and managers who first defined clear, actionable KPIs—such as scam victim rate per thousand active users—and proxy metrics to enable timely monitoring despite reporting delays. Initial solutions involved manual cohort reviews and simple heuristic business rules drawn from expert knowledge to detect suspicious behaviors, acknowledging limitations in rule-based systems due to high false positives and scammers’ rapid adaptation. The team invested heavily in human-labeled data and developed tooling to rigorously evaluate rule performance, building stakeholder confidence prior to deploying adaptive machine learning models capable of capturing nuanced fraud patterns and maintaining effectiveness through regular retraining. This structured approach allowed scaling from manual interventions to automated semantic retrieval-based fraud detection, ensuring continuous measurement, cross-department visibility, and strategic prioritization of metrics to optimize user protection and operational impact.

BlaBlaCar addressed fraud detection challenges affecting trip publications and bookings by building a machine learning pipeline tailored for near real-time scoring within an event-driven Kafka architecture, ensuring no disruption to user experience. The system integrates both expert rules and ML models to compute fraud scores on member events, which downstream services then use to take actions like canceling trips or requesting additional verification. Critical to success was the meticulous management of features and labels: serving features are sourced from a real-time feature store fed by Kafka event projections, with careful engineering to maintain feature consistency between training and serving phases and avoid data leakage, while labels are aggregated from multiple sources including manual reviews and rule-based detections, consolidated into a unified label table for accurate training and reporting. This design enables iterative improvements with reliable data quality control, emphasizing distinct responsibilities between software engineers (feature quality) and data scientists (label quality) to increase fraud detection efficacy without compromising the platform’s operational stability.

Building Boba AI addresses the business challenge of augmenting early-stage product strategy and generative ideation processes with an LLM-powered co-pilot designed for product strategists and innovation teams. The web application mediates user interactions with OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 via structured UI workflows that guide prompt engineering, enabling research signal analysis, creative matrix ideation, scenario building, strategy formulation, concept generation, and storyboard visualization. Key data constraints include the need to incorporate up-to-date external knowledge beyond the LLM’s training cutoff by combining real-time web search APIs with in-memory vector stores for embedding-based retrieval, supporting dynamic content summarization and source attribution. Boba leverages patterns such as templated prompts, structured JSON responses, real-time streamed outputs, select-and-carry context for multi-threaded exploration, contextual conversation fallback, chain-of-thought reasoning, iterative user feedback loops, and embedded external knowledge integration to produce high-quality, relevant, and explainable strategy insights and creative concepts rapidly, effectively scaling and accelerating divergent thinking and strategic innovation workflows.

Instacart developed Ava, an internal AI assistant leveraging OpenAI’s GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 models, to scale employee productivity across engineering and non-engineering teams by addressing the challenge of efficient information access, code development, and communication improvement. Initially designed to aid developers with coding, debugging, and testing via a ChatGPT-like web interface that supports conversation search and automatic model upgrades, Ava rapidly expanded usage to operations, recruiting, marketing, and HR users by introducing prompt templates and conversation sharing features. Integration with Slack, including thread summarization through commands like “@Ava summarize,” reduced cognitive load in managing lengthy discussions and boosted adoption. Ava’s continual enhancement focuses on integrating internal knowledge retrieval and code execution capabilities to handle complex tasks more effectively, with plans to expose its API company-wide to embed AI throughout workflows, thereby expecting substantial gains in productivity, knowledge sharing, and operational efficiency.

The business problem addresses enabling users across iOS, macOS, and iPadOS to instantly and automatically isolate subjects in images regardless of object class, supporting a broad range of use cases like photo editing and live sticker creation. Intended users include consumers interacting with apps such as Photos, Preview, and Safari who require low-latency, on-device salient object segmentation without reliance on fixed semantic categories. The proposed solution employs an efficient convolutional neural network, based on EfficientNet v2 encoder and multi-branch decoder, running on Apple Neural Engine or GPU, producing pixel-wise alpha mattes at 512×512 resolution with confidence gating to ensure result reliability. Key data strategies involve combining synthetic and real-world datasets with on-the-fly foreground-background composition, mitigating bias across demographics, and applying content-aware upsampling for fine detail preservation. The expected outcome is a seamless, power-efficient user experience delivering high-quality, class-agnostic object extractions in under 10 milliseconds on modern Apple devices, validated through both quantitative metrics and human evaluation to ensure fairness and perceptual quality.

Instagram’s Explore recommendation system addresses the business problem of delivering highly relevant and engaging content in real time from billions of media items to hundreds of millions of daily users. To meet this challenge, data scientists and ML engineers use a multi-stage ranking pipeline involving retrieval, lightweight first-stage ranking, heavier second-stage ranking, and final reranking with business-rule filters. The retrieval stage employs a Two Tower neural network model that independently embeds users and items for efficient caching and scalable approximate nearest neighbors search, sourcing candidates both from heuristics and ML-based real-time and precomputed sources. Ranking models—continuously fine-tuned hourly—leverage multi-task neural networks predicting engagement-related probabilities, combined into a value model to balance metrics like click and like likelihoods, while final reranking applies integrity and diversity constraints. Parameter tuning utilizes Bayesian optimization and offline simulations leveraging historical metrics to optimize system performance despite complexity and scale. This advanced ML-driven, cache-optimized architecture enables Instagram Explore to maintain flexibility, scalability, and adaptability in surfacing personalized content within stringent latency and load constraints.

OLX addressed the business problem of users lacking accurate delivery time estimates for Pay&Ship transactions, which impeded buyer trust and conversion in its classified e-commerce platform where sellers are individuals and delivery involves both seller handoff time and carrier transit time. Targeting buyers deciding on delivery options, the solution involved exploratory data analysis identifying the carrier as the largest contributor to delivery duration and other factors like order day, region, and distance. A simple baseline model predicting delivery time ranges per carrier was first deployed and validated through A/B testing to assess user impact. Subsequently, a more sophisticated machine learning approach using CatBoost with quantile regression was developed to predict delivery time intervals, improving accuracy to 81% and reducing early and late deliveries versus baseline. The model was batch-predicted due to challenges in accessing real-time buyer data, and the entire pipeline was productionized with automated data processing, model training, deployment, and monitoring infrastructure. Expected outcomes include enhanced buyer experience, increased Pay&Ship conversions, and reduced churn from poor delivery experiences, with next steps focusing on further experimentation, scaling, and performance monitoring.

Netflix faced the business problem of managing numerous machine learning models tailored for different recommendation use-cases—such as notifications, related items, search, and category exploration—resulting in high system complexity, technical debt, and maintenance overhead. Their intended users are both internal ML engineering teams, responsible for maintaining and updating recommendation pipelines, and end-users receiving personalized content. The proposed solution consolidates multiple bespoke ML models into a single multi-task machine learning model with a unified offline pipeline that harmonizes diverse request contexts into a joint schema augmented by a categorical task_type variable, enabling joint training across use-cases. Online serving adapts to varied latency, throughput, availability, and business logic requirements by deploying the consolidated model in multiple environments with configurable inference settings behind a use-case-agnostic API. Key data considerations include labeled interaction logs from distinct UI canvases unified via stratification and feature vectors with sentinel defaults for missing values. Expected outcomes include reduced codebase complexity, improved maintainability, accelerated feature rollout across recommendation tasks, extensibility for new use-cases, and enhanced system robustness through shared knowledge transfer, while carefully managing risks of cross-task regression.

The use case focuses on building an enterprise large language model (LLM) application exemplified by GitHub Copilot, targeting developers who need to write code faster and more efficiently without changing their existing workflows. The solution involved identifying a specific, impactful problem—coding function completions within integrated development environments (IDEs)—and iteratively refining AI-generated whole-function suggestions through extensive user feedback, A/B testing, and scaling infrastructure. Key challenges included ensuring consistent and secure code outputs despite LLMs’ probabilistic nature, optimizing computational costs, and managing community concerns about code originality and licensing. By emphasizing rapid prototyping, dogfooding, integrating into existing tools, and leveraging diverse user feedback, the team achieved general availability with high-quality, context-aware coding assistance that improved developer productivity and was adaptable across multiple programming languages.

Dailymotion addresses the business challenge of combating filter bubbles in video recommendations by developing an opinion-based recommender system aimed at its mobile app users who seek diverse and stimulating content while engaging with different viewpoints. The solution enhances an existing multi-stage recommender architecture by introducing a two-step process: Candidate Generation retrieves videos on similar topics using vector embeddings generated from multilingual textual metadata and automatically transcribed video audio via OpenAI's Whisper model, indexed in the Qdrant vector database for efficient approximate nearest neighbor search; Re-ranking then orders these candidates based on opinion intensity scores derived from sentiment analysis performed by Google’s PaLM language model on video transcripts, emphasizing videos that express strong or divergent opinions. This approach leverages semantic retrieval through text embeddings and opinion mining to present personalized yet perspective-challenging recommendations, ultimately promoting user exposure to a broader range of ideas and fostering debate on the platform.

Wayfair addresses the challenge of managing multiple machine learning models for sending millions of daily marketing emails and push notifications by developing Griffin, a reinforcement learning–based notification governance model that unifies send decisions across channels and notification types. Targeting marketing and engineering teams, Griffin uses contextual bandits to balance exploration and optimization of send/no-send actions at the individual notification level, incorporating features like campaign context and customer behavior triggers. By leveraging real-time feedback from email engagement metrics (clicks and unsubscribes) as rewards, Griffin continuously updates its policy, eliminating repeated retraining and A/B testing, while adapting to dynamic customer response patterns. Currently deployed for real-time behavior-triggered emails, Griffin is designed for scalable expansion to daily sales emails and push messages, aiming to optimize cross-channel communication relevance, increase customer engagement, reduce unsubscriptions, and improve long-term conversion rates through personalized, coordinated notification strategies supported by real-time and batch feature processing infrastructure.

Whatnot addresses the challenge of maintaining a safe live shopping marketplace by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) alongside a centralized rule engine to enhance trust and safety. The primary users are the marketplace’s community and trust and safety team who face issues such as scams, harassment, and fraud that are difficult to detect through isolated message analysis. The solution integrates multimodal content moderation including message text and OCR-extracted image data to analyze entire conversation exchanges, user behaviors, and account metadata, enabling nuanced context comprehension beyond scalar rule thresholds. LLMs estimate scam likelihoods and provide detailed explanations, feeding into an augmented rule engine (Rule Engine++) which automates enforcement actions—ranging from warnings to suspensions—with human review for ambiguous cases. This hybrid human-AI workflow achieves over 95% proactive scam detection with high precision and recall, continuously adapting to evolving fraudulent patterns to safeguard user interactions and platform integrity.

Dropbox addressed the business challenge of inconsistent and ambiguous date formats in file names, which hindered effective organization and retrieval for users leveraging naming conventions. Intended for Dropbox users who require automated, consistent file naming, the proposed solution employs a supervised machine learning classification model—built on a fine-tuned, optimized DistilRoberta transformer—that identifies and labels individual date components (year, month, day) in file names using tokenization (SentencePiece) and IOB tagging. Training data combined manual annotation of diverse real employee files with synthetically generated samples to cover varied formats and reduce overfitting, while model pruning and quantization reduced inference latency for better user experience. The outcome was a 40% improvement in renamed files over rule-based methods and increased feature adoption, facilitating automated, accurate date extraction to enhance file organization workflows at scale.

This use case addresses the business problem of improving recommender systems (RecSys) by explicitly modeling user choice behavior, targeting researchers and system designers focused on user-centric recommendation. Instead of treating RecSys as a pattern recognition task, the proposed solution advocates for defining and studying explicit user models that separate browsing (information gathering) and consumption (decision-making) policies, incorporating user rationality and heterogeneity through unobservable private types modeled probabilistically. The system aims to capture two key recommendation effects: the "shortcut effect," which reduces friction by guiding users quickly to desired items, and the "information effect," which influences user utility by exposing users to new items, additional features, or reminders, thereby altering product ranking and choices. Important constraints include focusing on short-term user response without modeling long-term preference evolution and acknowledging the black-box nature of current bandit and reinforcement learning approaches. Expected outcomes include a unified theoretical framework to better explain and predict offline-online metric discrepancies, improved system interpretability, enhanced measurement of recommendation incrementality, and stronger integration with econometric and mechanism design principles to address ethical and economic issues, ultimately enabling recommender systems that provide more informed and personalized user experiences.

Pinterest addresses the challenge of delivering relevant, personalized recommendations when users closely engage with Pins by improving the training foundation of their Closeup Recommendation Ranker, used by their recommendation engineers and data scientists. They implement a hybrid data logging system combining backend and frontend logging to efficiently capture rich, high-quality training data while minimizing storage. They improve sampling strategies through configurable jobs that handle petabyte-scale datasets, enabling nuanced control over training data distribution to reduce bias and enhance content safety, evidenced by broad engagement gains in A/B tests. The solution includes an Auto-Retraining Framework (ARF) that automates periodic model retraining, validation, and deployment to counteract model performance degradation due to feature drift and evolving user preferences, featuring knowledge distillation techniques and synchronized deployment of calibrated and uncalibrated models. This end-to-end system reduces manual intervention, accelerates training workflows from hours to minutes, and maintains consistent improvements in recommendation quality and user engagement across Pinterest’s platform.

Instacart addresses the business challenge of personalizing product search and ranking across a vast product space to improve customer engagement and purchasing metrics, primarily targeting e-commerce shoppers. The solution employs Contextual Bandit (CB) models, which personalize recommendations by leveraging user and query context to select the best item ranking or ranking formula—balancing objectives like relevance, popularity, price, and availability—out of a large and complex action space that precludes treating each possible product list as a discrete action. To overcome data sparsity and scaling constraints, Instacart uses strategies such as defining a discrete set of ranking formulas as actions and applying advanced CB training frameworks like the X-learner to estimate treatment effects, alongside counterfactual evaluation techniques like Inverse Propensity Sampling and Doubly Robust estimators to assess model impact offline. The CB models are trained using tools like XGBoost for fast and powerful learning and RLlib for scalable reinforcement learning, enabling robust exploration and exploitation in both discrete and continuous action spaces. Deploying these models in production has yielded statistically significant lifts (around 0.6-0.66%) in key metrics like cart adds per search, validating the approach for personalized, multi-objective ranking in real-world large-action recommendation environments.

LinkedIn addresses the challenge of detecting viral spam content to maintain a safe and professional environment for its members by deploying a combination of proactive and reactive AI models. Intended for platform moderators and automated systems, these models leverage deep neural networks and Boosted Trees classifiers trained on features related to content type, polarity, spam signals, member network influence, user activity, and engagement patterns such as likes, shares, and comments. Proactive models act immediately when content appears, predicting potential virality and spam to allow prompt filtering or human review, while reactive models monitor engagement signals over time to prevent further spread. Despite data scarcity of viral spam instances, these approaches have collectively reduced views on spam content by 7.3% and policy-violating content by 12%, ultimately enhancing user experience by limiting exposure to unwanted viral spam on LinkedIn’s professional feed.

This use case addresses the business problem of ensuring compliance with separation of duties in software development, a challenge for developers, compliance, and audit teams who currently rely on manual and time-consuming reviews. The intended users are software developers and compliance teams within enterprises. The proposed solution leverages generative AI, specifically GitHub Copilot for Pull Requests, to automate and optimize code review and compliance processes by generating pull request descriptions, embedding AI-powered tags, and providing AI-assisted code review suggestions that help identify risks, technical debt, and security vulnerabilities early. Important data and constraints include adherence to PCI-DSS requirements emphasizing separation of development/test and production functions, as well as compatibility with existing DevOps workflows like Infrastructure as Code and Policy-as-Code. The expected outcome is a more efficient, compliant, and developer-friendly workflow that reduces manual effort, accelerates delivery, maintains audit readiness, and allows human reviewers to focus on high-value, risk-based compliance activities.

The Personalized ‘Complete the Look’ (CTL) model addresses the challenge in fashion and home e-commerce of guiding users to discover cohesive, stylized outfits or collections centered on an anchor item viewed by the customer.
