Intended for shoppers on platforms like Walmart, the solution leverages multiple machine learning algorithms including candidate selection from complementary item recommendations filtered by age, gender, and season; look definition based on hierarchical product types and super product types to formulate coherent multi-item outfits; and outfit style matching using triplet learning on visual embeddings (e.g., CLIP) for compatibility beyond co-purchase signals. The system integrates user interaction feedback (clicks, add-to-carts) to refine look generation and employs a search-and-refine expansion approach to scale human-curated styles across large catalogs by identifying visually similar items and filtering for compatibility constraints such as size and demographic attributes. The expected outcome is enhanced product discovery, increased shopper confidence, higher conversion rates, and more complete multi-item baskets, creating a more cohesive and personalized shopping experience in style-driven categories.

DoorDash addressed the business problem of reducing Dasher wait times caused by variability in restaurant food preparation start times and processes, impacting delivery efficiency and Dasher earnings. The intended users include Dashers and merchants in the food delivery ecosystem who are affected by mismatches in food readiness and Dasher arrival. Their solution evolved from a heuristic-based Auto Order Release (AOR) system—which delayed sending orders to kitchens until Dashers neared the restaurant—to a dynamic, ML-driven approach that estimates optimal order release timing for each delivery. The machine learning models, notably LightGBM predictors tailored to unique marketplace features, leverage real-time data on food prep times and Dasher arrival to minimize waiting without degrading food quality or overall delivery time. This required extensive cross-functional collaboration, new architectural capabilities for dynamic decision-making per order rather than store-level heuristics, and a phased rollout starting with heuristic MVP experiments to gather real-world data. The expected outcomes were measurable reductions in Dasher wait time, improved merchant throughput, and scalable onboarding of merchants, achieved through iterative ML model tuning aligned with operational metrics and continuous experimentation within DoorDash's production environment.

DoorDash faced the challenge of accurately tracking merchant operational status to prevent order cancellations caused by discrepancies between store open hours and actual store availability, negatively impacting customers, Dashers, and merchants. To address this, they implemented a "Dasher reports store closed" (DRSC) feature allowing Dashers to report closures with photographic evidence, which previously relied on costly, manual verification. They upgraded this heuristic with a machine learning model, specifically a LightGBM classifier, combining features from store and Dasher histories, timestamps, and an image classifier summarizing storefront photos to compute the probability that a store is closed upon a DRSC report. This probabilistic approach enables automated, scalable decisions: high closure probability results in canceling orders and pausing merchants, low probabilities prompt reassignment of Dashers, and intermediate probabilities lead to cancellations only. Deployment of this ML-driven system has reduced unnecessary cancellations, improving user experience, merchant revenue, and Dasher opportunities, demonstrating the value of optimizing rule-based operational workflows with statistical decision-making models in large-scale logistics platforms.

Coupang addressed the business problem of efficiently allocating limited unloading docks (slots) for inbound delivery trucks at fulfillment centers, targeting logistics managers and vendors as users, by developing a machine learning solution that predicts the optimal number of trucks needed per inbound shipment. Utilizing over two years of logistics and inbound request data, domain expert insights, and feature engineering, they trained a LightGBM model—favored for handling large categorical datasets and fast training—with hyperparameters optimized via Bayesian optimization, to achieve accurate truck demand forecasts. Integrated into the vendor reservation system through AWS SageMaker, the model balances underprediction (risking delays) and overprediction (wasting dock resources), ultimately reducing vendor delivery date changes by 67.9%, decreasing underprediction from 8.71% to 2.53% and overprediction from 44.45% to 5.04%, thereby streamlining inbound slot usage, minimizing costs, and enabling timely product availability.

The Spotify Track Neural Recommender System addresses the challenge of automatically continuing music playlists to enhance user discovery and listening experience by recommending songs that complement existing playlists' styles and themes, targeting music streaming consumers and playlist creators. It leverages a large-scale dataset of over one million Spotify playlists represented as a bipartite graph between playlists and tracks, focusing on a highly connected 30-core subgraph for computational feasibility. The system employs graph neural networks (GNNs) such as LightGCN, Graph Attention Network (GATConv), and GraphSAGE (SAGEConv) to learn node embeddings that capture playlist-track similarities, facilitating transductive link prediction via masked edges for train, validation, and testing splits. By optimizing embeddings with Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss and employing random and hard negative sampling strategies, the models predict track recommendations through dot-product similarity scores to effectively continue playlists. Evaluation using Recall@300 demonstrates that more complex GNN convolution methods like SAGEConv outperform simpler models, improving recommendation quality while visualizing embedding clusters reveals nuanced playlist structure. This approach showcases the promise of graph neural methods in personalized music recommendation, influencing features like Spotify's Enhance and Apple’s Autoplay for seamless playlist experience.

Spotify addressed the challenge of generating scalable, low-latency podcast previews for millions of episodes by integrating Podz's ML pipeline into a managed, distributed data processing system using Google Dataflow with Apache Beam. Targeting content discovery users who need quick audio teasers beyond static visuals, the solution processes raw audio and transcriptions through an ensemble of diverse ML models (including transformers and sound event detection) built on heterogeneous frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, all orchestrated within Dockerized custom containers to handle complex dependencies. Key constraints included handling a rapidly growing catalog with hundreds of thousands of new episodes daily, maintaining multiple pipeline versions (production, staging, fallback), optimizing GPU utilization for latency and throughput, and overcoming dependency and SDK upgrade errors. Transitioning from batch to streaming pipelines via the Klio framework reduced preview generation latency from two hours to under four minutes, dramatically improving timeliness for time-sensitive content. Continuous monitoring and pipeline tuning ensure reliability and resource efficiency, leveraging Dataflow features like autoscaling and future enhancements such as Dataflow Prime and the RunInference API for improved resource allocation and inference batching.

Pinterest addressed the business problem of high advertiser churn, particularly among small and medium business (SMB) advertisers, by developing a machine learning (ML) solution intended for use by their Sales Account Managers to proactively predict and prevent churn. The proposed solution uses a Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) model, trained on over 200 aggregated features spanning advertiser performance metrics, budget utilization, campaign settings, and account properties, to predict the likelihood that an active advertiser (defined as having spent in the last 7 days) will churn in the next 14 days (defined as no spend in the last 7 days). Feature contributions to predictions are interpreted using SHAP values, which help sales prioritize outreach by understanding key drivers of churn risk. The model output categorizes accounts into high, medium, or low churn risk to guide sales efforts strategically. In a North America SMB experiment, this ML-powered proactive approach yielded a statistically significant 24% reduction in churn rate for managed accounts compared to reactive methods, with predictive performance metrics (AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, precision, recall) closely matching offline evaluations. Future work includes exploring sequential models like LSTMs and Transformers to better capture temporal advertising behaviors and reduce manual feature engineering.

Lyft's recommendation system addresses the challenge of optimizing ride mode selection amid a broad and growing portfolio of transportation options, targeting riders who seek personalized, efficient booking experiences while balancing marketplace supply and demand. Leveraging machine learning models such as LightGBM with multi-class classification and lambda rank objectives, the system predicts each rider's propensity to convert to specific ride modes by incorporating rich contextual features including location, time, supply-demand signals, and user ride history. It dynamically ranks and preselects optimal modes to reduce cognitive overload and expedite ride requests, solving problems like overchoice, cold start for new modes via post-processing adjustments, and dynamic business goals beyond mere conversion rates, such as ride reliability and market balance. This hybrid, real-time approach underpins features like the One-Tap module and post-request cross-sells to improve matching efficiency and rider satisfaction, with ongoing enhancements planned via reinforcement learning to capture longer-term user engagement.

DoorDash aims to enhance its delivery platform by leveraging Generative AI to address five key areas: aiding customers in task completion (e.g., automated cart building, order tracking, and voice ordering), improving personalized discovery through knowledge graph-based recommendations, generating customized content and merchandising such as dynamic menus and targeted promotions, extracting structured data from unstructured sources like receipts and menus via OCR, and boosting employee productivity by automating routine tasks including SQL query generation and document drafting. These AI-driven solutions intend to reduce friction in the customer journey, increase merchant revenue, and optimize operational efficiency, all while carefully managing data privacy, security, and ethical considerations to prevent bias and protect user information.

The business problem addressed is managing duplicate issues and backlog clutter in large team workflows, where duplicate bug reports lead to inefficiencies and redundant work among engineers. Intended users include engineers, support teams, and triage personnel working within Linear workspaces and customer support integrations. The proposed solution leverages large language models (LLMs) and vector embeddings to semantically encode issue text, enabling efficient similarity searches based on cosine similarity rather than keyword matching. This is integrated during issue creation and in triage/support tools, surfacing related issues early to prevent duplicates. Important constraints include handling tens of millions of issues with performant similarity search, solved by partitioning embeddings stored in PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension on Google Cloud, balancing scalability, cost, and operational complexity. The expected outcome is a streamlined workflow reducing duplicate issue creation, consolidating related customer support tickets, and improving backlog organization for engineering and support teams.

Loblaw Digital addresses the challenge of maintaining comprehensive, up-to-date documentation for over 3,000 dbt models used across its analytics and business intelligence teams, where manual annotation is time-consuming and often incomplete, causing confusion for business users unfamiliar with the data. The intended users are analytics engineers and data analysts who rely on clear model descriptions to understand data transformations and lineage. Their solution leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) hosted on platforms like Vertex AI to automatically generate detailed documentation by ingesting dbt model schemas from manifest.json files without accessing underlying data, thus preserving data privacy and integrity. This AI-driven documentation enriches the SQL and schema metadata with natural-language descriptions of model logic, dependencies, and columns, significantly reducing documentation debt and increasing productivity in managing the evolving ELT dbt framework. The expected outcome is streamlined workflows, improved data transparency for non-technical stakeholders, and enhanced collaboration within Loblaw’s data organization.

Coupang addresses the challenge of accurate word segmentation for character-based Asian languages like Korean, Chinese, and Japanese in its e-commerce platform, where traditional supervised segmentation methods fail due to lack of labeled data and unique linguistic features such as omitted delimiters and postpositions. Their solution, intended for improving search result relevance and personalized recommendations, employs an unsupervised, fully automated word segmentation system that leverages a massive dataset of over one trillion unlabeled product titles to train a character embedding model and two competing bidirectional recurrent neural language models. These models estimate the probabilities of character sequences from forward and backward contexts to dynamically determine word boundaries without human annotation. The expected outcome is improved segmentation accuracy tailored to e-commerce product titles, enhancing customer search experience and potentially increasing sales by providing more precise keyword extraction and query understanding across multiple Asian languages.

Coupang Eats addresses the complex online-to-offline food delivery market challenges involving customers, merchants, and delivery partners (EDPs) through advanced data science and machine learning solutions. The platform targets optimizing order assignment (OA) by modeling it as a bipartite graph matching problem that maximizes matching scores based on multiple factors like pickup distance, EDP preferences, and predicted wait times, enabling real-time, globally optimal dispatch decisions. Pricing strategies combine static base fees and mission-based incentives with dynamic regional and task-level pricing adjusted via predictive models accounting for supply-demand fluctuations and EDP acceptance sensitivity to maintain cost efficiency and delivery quality. Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA) predictions for food preparation and delivery leverage regression and deep neural networks to forecast times accurately and manage customer and EDP expectations. Additional challenges such as balancing supply-demand via predictive triggers and optimizing merchant delivery scopes using isochrones based on real travel distances further enhance operational efficiency and customer conversion. The integrated approach combines predictive modeling with multi-objective global optimization to deliver fast, cost-effective food delivery while balancing competing business goals and stakeholder experiences in a dynamic environment.

In large-scale software projects with lengthy test runtimes causing costly delays and slow developer feedback, machine learning can rapidly predict test failures at commit time by training supervised models on integrated source control and test execution logs, enabling developers to receive near-instantaneous feedback before tests complete; this system, validated on tens of thousands of real test cases with median accuracy around 78%, also supports optimizing test suite execution order by prioritizing tests most likely to fail, thereby reducing time to first failure by about 16% and overall runtime by roughly 10%, which translates to significant resource savings such as fewer required test machines. Additionally, integrating heterogeneous data sources permits resolving defect assignment ambiguities in multi-team environments by linking test cases to defects and analyzing historical fix patterns to recommend responsible teams with 75% recall, mitigating "defect hot potato" issues. The approach hinges on high data quality and traceability across diverse repositories, necessitates scalable system design for continuous data ingestion and model inference, and benefits from change management to align technical stakeholders with its value.

Vorwerk’s Cookidoo platform for its Thermomix smart cooker serves over 5 million users worldwide with 80,000+ recipes in 12 languages, facing the challenge of delivering personalized recipe recommendations that cater to diverse regional tastes and dietary preferences, thereby enhancing user engagement and reducing decision fatigue. The intended users are home cooks seeking tailored culinary suggestions to inspire healthy and efficient meal preparation. The proposed solution employs matrix factorization-based recommender systems trained on implicit user interaction data (e.g., recipe usage timestamps) rather than explicit ratings, with one model trained per language to respect regional and cultural recipe variations, combined with rule-based filters to enforce regional relevance and measurement systems. Privacy and GDPR compliance constraints guide careful handling of user data. The team selected the LightFM library for its rapid deployment capabilities and ability to incorporate side information to improve recommendations iteratively, opting against complex distributed training or deep learning models due to data scale and complexity considerations. The expected outcome is a scalable, privacy-conscious personalized recommendation service that improves user satisfaction and platform loyalty by making “what to cook?” decisions easier and more enjoyable.

Didact AI addresses the challenge of consistent stock picking to outperform the market, targeting investors seeking data-driven weekly stock recommendations. The solution is a productionized machine learning pipeline combining extensive feature engineering on multimodal financial data—including price/volume, options, earnings transcripts, and macroeconomic indicators—with market regime and sentiment analysis to contextualize patterns. Using advanced data ingestion and a multi-store architecture (DuckDB, Redis), the system generates over 1000 engineered features per stock daily for 4000+ US equities, processed within about 14 minutes on AWS infrastructure. A gradient boosted decision tree model (xgboost), retrained daily, forecasts stocks with a high probability of superior risk-adjusted returns, supported by a regime detection model and explainability via SHAP values. The ML Ops framework emphasizes monitoring, diagnostics, and backups to maintain performance amid market regime shifts. Despite achieving consistent outperformance versus the S&P 500 during its operational period, the newsletter was discontinued due to product-market fit challenges influenced by investors’ behavioral biases in volatile markets.

Tubi addresses the challenge of extracting actionable insights from large-scale user text feedback—including Net Promoter Score (NPS) comments and customer support tickets—by applying pre-trained natural language processing (NLP) models for semantic classification. Intended for product managers and customer support teams, the solution employs Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) to generate embeddings that represent the semantic meaning of feedback entries, which are then input into LightGBM classifiers trained on manually labeled data to categorize comments into predefined buckets (e.g., content, ads, feature issues, requests, complaints). This automated categorization enables scalable daily trend tracking via dashboards, facilitating prioritized product improvements and more efficient support ticket routing, thus saving time and improving response quality despite growing volumes of unstructured text data.

ASOS addresses the business challenge of efficiently managing promotional pricing ("markdown") in fashion e-commerce, where demand is volatile due to fast-changing trends and inventory is purchased well in advance. Intended users include retail pricing operations teams and machine learning scientists. The proposed solution comprises two machine learning-based markdown engines: Ithax, a cold start optimizer focusing on supply-side objectives without demand estimation to control financial risk and bootstrap data collection, and Promotheus, a full markdown optimization framework using causal inference and price elasticity models to forecast sales and profits, with rigorous offline and real-world validation to overcome partial information constraints inherent in price optimization. These systems operate on large-scale product and sales data, employing multi-objective optimization to balance stock value and profit margins, ultimately delivering substantial profitability gains—86% for Promotheus and 79% for Ithax—over manual strategies, and have been successfully deployed at scale on ASOS.com.

ASOS addresses the challenge of surfacing the right products from a vast and frequently updated catalog of about 100,000 fashion items to its 26.7 million global customers by employing a scalable, low-latency personalization system based on deep learning embeddings. The AI team generates meaningful customer and product embeddings using neural collaborative filtering on rich interaction data (views, purchases, save-for-laters) and content features like images and text to overcome cold-start issues. These shared latent representations enable multiple downstream ranking tasks for personalized product recommendations across browsing touchpoints—such as the "For You" tab, category/search pages, and "You Might Also Like" carousels—by computing similarity scores efficiently during inference. The system integrates technologies like Databricks, TensorFlow 2, Azure Machine Learning, and NVIDIA Triton to support fast iteration, experimentation, and high traffic loads during sales events, ultimately enhancing user engagement through increased clicks and purchases by reducing browsing friction and delivering tailored shopping experiences.

At CARS24, the challenge of subjective vehicle image evaluations leading to costly errors and poor customer experience motivated the development of a blur classifier to detect image quality artefacts, specifically blur, which negatively impact computer vision model accuracy. The intended users are the data scientists and machine learning systems analyzing car photos for defect detection. To ensure only high-quality, artefact-free images are used for model training and inference, they designed a lightweight, accurate algorithm based on discrete cosine transform (DCT) analysis of 8x8 image blocks, extracting 18 statistical features from low, medium, and high frequency regions to classify images as blurry or sharp. This approach achieves 91.06% accuracy with a fast 12ms processing time per 1080x1920 image on a single CPU, improving the procurement and inspection pipeline by standardizing image quality assessment and reducing false positives and negatives in vehicle damage estimation.

The Monolith system addresses the business challenge of building a scalable, real-time recommendation platform critical for time-sensitive user feedback in domains like short-video ranking and online ads, targeting industrial users who require instant adaptation to dynamic and sparse user behavior data characterized by concept drift. The solution introduces a collisionless embedding table, implemented via a Cuckoo HashMap that avoids damaging embedding collisions common in fixed-size hash approaches, alongside a highly optimized online training architecture that integrates streaming engines for low-latency feature joining and incrementally synchronizes sparse parameter updates from training to serving with minute-level frequency, while trading off strict parameter version consistency and tolerating occasional parameter server failures to balance model quality and system reliability. Empirical results on public and internal datasets demonstrate that Monolith’s collisionless embeddings yield significant improvements in online AUC metrics compared to collision-based hashing, and frequent online training and parameter synchronization lead to superior real-time recommendation accuracy, validating the approach for production-scale recommender systems under constraints of memory footprint, computational overhead, and system fault tolerance.

DoorDash addresses the business problem of efficiently expanding its merchant selection to match customer demand across diverse markets by leveraging machine learning to identify high-value off-platform merchants. Intended for merchant sales teams, the solution entails developing scalable XGBoost models trained on features capturing consumer intent, merchant attributes, and performance labels reflecting merchants' true potential within a consistent time window post-onboarding. The system incorporates rigorous feature engineering, segmentation by merchant type and tenure, continuous model validation with metrics like weighted decile CPE and decile rank score, and interpretability using Shapley values. Daily predictions rank off-platform merchants by success potential, enabling sales prioritization and accurate calculation of the addressable market. This data-driven approach enhances lead identification, resource allocation, and market expansion, ultimately improving operational efficiency and customer satisfaction in DoorDash’s food delivery platform.

GitHub addresses the business problem of detecting security vulnerabilities in source code to prevent malicious exploitation by integrating machine learning with its CodeQL code scanning tool, targeting developers who manage code repositories. The proposed solution leverages manually crafted CodeQL queries as ground truth to label massive datasets of code snippets from public repositories, training deep learning models to classify snippets as vulnerable or safe, even uncovering risks in previously unseen libraries. By extracting rich, code-representative features beyond raw syntax and feeding them into neural networks, the system identifies vulnerabilities missed by manual queries with about 80% recall and 60% precision. This semantic retrieval approach enhances code security alerts during pull requests without requiring GPUs at inference, running transparently within GitHub Actions, thereby improving developer productivity and code safety across JavaScript, TypeScript, and planned expansion to additional languages.

LinkedIn addressed the challenge of improving the relevance and agility of Post search, used by members to find industry-related content amid diverse and growing posts, by decoupling their Post search tech stack from the Feed ecosystem to simplify architecture and enable faster iterations. Their solution employed a multi-aspect First Pass Ranker composed of lightweight independent ML models optimizing for query-document relevance, static quality, personalization, engagement, and freshness, followed by a Second Pass Ranker leveraging neural networks for deeper personalization and a Diversity re-ranker to enhance content variety and serendipitous discovery. Important constraints included latency limits demanding efficient ranking at scale and the integration of product-driven priorities like diversity and freshness. Internal tools validated model improvements via descriptive statistics, rule-based testing, and crowdsourced relevance ratings. This re-architecture resulted in significant improvements in developer productivity, latency reduction, personalized and engaging search results, and increased user interactions such as click-through rates and messaging, demonstrating a successful, explainable, and extensible ML-powered semantic retrieval system tailored for LinkedIn’s unique content and user engagement context.

This use case addresses the challenge faced by retail demand planners in estimating the profitability and sales uplift of past in-store promotions, a key issue since actual baseline sales without promotions are unknown. To solve this, data scientists developed and deployed a counterfactual forecasting model, initially using Prophet and later XGBoost for efficiency and accuracy, trained on out-of-promotion sales data to predict hypothetical sales baselines during promotion periods. The model inputs include enriched sales data combined with detailed promotion descriptors and temporal features, achieving about 90% forecast accuracy at a product family-day granularity. By comparing predicted baselines to actual sales, the uplift and return on investment of past promotions can be estimated despite the lack of ground truth and complexities like overlapping promotions or long-duration campaigns. This a posteriori analysis aids planners in evaluating historical campaign effectiveness and sets the foundation for predicting future promotions’ performance and optimizing promotional strategies to maximize business metrics such as ROI.

eBay addresses the challenge of providing personalized item recommendations to its 152 million users browsing 1.5 billion listings by developing a large-scale, low-latency deep learning retrieval system that leverages natural language processing to generate embeddings for users and items. Intended for data scientists and engineers operating in high-traffic ecommerce environments, the solution employs a two-tower model to create user and item embeddings that facilitate k-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) or Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) searches for rapid recommendation retrieval. The system evolves through three phases: an initial offline batch-processing setup that precomputes embeddings with some delay; a hybrid phase that introduces a real-time KNN search service to reduce latency; and a fully near-real-time architecture that integrates streaming event capture via Kafka, real-time model inference with Nvidia Triton on GPU, and real-time embedding updates to serve fresh, personalized recommendations within seconds. Key data components include user click histories, item metadata, and embedding vectors stored in fast-access caches like Couchbase, while operational constraints involve balancing latency, throughput, and system complexity. The expected outcome is a scalable, production-grade recommendation engine that continuously updates with user behavior and item availability, significantly enhancing the relevance and timeliness of ecommerce recommendations.

GoFood addresses the critical business problem of accurately estimating food delivery times to improve customer satisfaction and conversion rates by developing Tensoba, a machine learning solution that predicts Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA) with minimal error relative to Actual Time of Arrival (ATA). Intended for millions of customers and over 300,000 merchants in Indonesia, Tensoba frames the ETA prediction as a regression problem using XGBoost models that incorporate both merchant-level historical data (such as average and percentile times for distinct order phases) and real-time order-level features including route distance, order value, and number of items. The model predicts delivery time by decomposing it into three components—order booking to driver arrival (T1), driver waiting at the restaurant (T2), and driver pickup to customer arrival (T3)—and either aggregating these or predicting them independently for improved accuracy. Evaluation metrics such as RMSE, MAE, and MAPE assess offline accuracy, while online metrics like compliance (ensuring ETA does not underpredict ATA) and conversion rate measure business impact post-deployment. Tensoba achieves a 23% MAPE improvement over baseline averages by updating predictions via batch processing and real-time APIs supported by Gojek’s data infrastructure, enabling dynamically tailored and reliable ETAs at both order discovery and checkout stages, enhancing user trust and engagement.

Airbnb addresses the business challenge of enhancing host and guest customer experiences through a unified Intelligent Automation Platform (AP) designed for conversational AI and agent automation. Intended for developers and non-technical business teams, AP models conversational workflows as Markov Decision Processes, facilitating consolidated, reusable actions and rapid product iteration via a drag-and-drop GUI called Flow Builder. The platform comprises an Event Orchestrator for channel-agnostic message normalization, a central Workflow Engine managing stateful workflow execution, an Action Store housing reusable actions—including complex machine learning-powered tasks—and the Flow Builder interface enabling collaborative workflow creation. By integrating diverse input channels such as messaging and automated calls, and supporting asynchronous internal events, AP standardizes task execution across systems, accelerates AI product development, democratizes access for business users, and scales intelligent customer support solutions to improve Airbnb’s service responsiveness and automation.

The Client Time Series Model (CTSM) addresses the business challenge of efficiently delivering personalized item recommendations across diverse channels, regions, and business lines for Stitch Fix by unifying and dynamically updating client state representations over time. Intended for recommendation engineers and data scientists, CTSM employs temporally-masked encoders and gated recurrent units to sequentially process timestamped client interaction events—both updates reflecting changes in client profile or behavior, and targets representing purchase probabilities—into time-safe client embeddings that adapt instantly to new data. Item embeddings are constructed via feature-sum embeddings used uniformly across contexts. This approach eliminates the maintenance overhead of multiple siloed models, leverages cross-domain learning, reduces computational resources, and accelerates development. Key outcomes include improved KPIs such as revenue and retention, immediate reflection of client updates in recommendations, and streamlined model infrastructure supporting rapid iteration.

Airbnb addresses the scalability and complexity challenges of customer support by leveraging large-scale AI text generation models that encode domain knowledge through extensive pre-training on past agent interactions, enabling unsupervised learning without costly data labeling. The primary users are Airbnb guests, hosts, and support agents, assisted via three innovative solutions: a prompt-based generative content recommendation model that ranks support documents more effectively than classification approaches; a real-time generative question-answering assistant that interprets user intent from ongoing conversations to suggest relevant templates while complying with policy; and a paraphrase model for the chatbot that rephrases user queries to confirm understanding and boost engagement, trained by filtering generic responses using clustering with Sentence-Transformers. These models collectively improve user experience by providing faster, more accurate resolutions and enhancing agent efficiency, demonstrating significant gains in business metrics and user engagement in large-scale production environments.

Mercado Libre faced the business problem of overfitting and high computational costs due to using over 4000 features in their fraud detection models, which complicated debugging, maintenance, and infrastructure expenses. The intended users were the machine learning teams seeking to improve model performance while preserving feature explainability and diversity, as features were crafted to address prior model deficiencies. The proposed unsupervised solution combined eigenvalue clipping and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to distinguish signal-bearing eigenvalues from noise by shuffling features to estimate noise distributions, then filtering the dataset to retain only signal components. This enabled hierarchical clustering of features based on a distance correlation matrix derived from the filtered data, allowing redundant features to be discarded without losing interpretability. Constraints included handling large datasets with non-stationary feature-target relationships but near-stationary feature-feature correlations. The expected outcome was a 70% reduction in features, 20% improvement in model performance by mitigating overfitting, and reduced model size and maintenance costs, translating into significant operational savings for Latin America’s largest marketplace.

LinkedIn addressed the business problem of improving ads click-through-rate (CTR) prediction, crucial for ad auction relevance and advertiser budget efficiency, by transitioning from a traditional GLMix model to a deep-learning-based solution targeting the ads domain's unique challenges. Intended users include LinkedIn members exposed to ads and advertisers paying for clicks. The proposed solution implements a three-tower neural network architecture: a deep tower capturing complete feature interactions among member, ad, and context embeddings via an end-to-end MLP served online; a wide tower for fast memorization of sparse ID features retrained hourly to capture ad performance trends; and a shallow tower for calibration to mitigate deep model over-prediction that could otherwise lead to inaccurate pricing. Important constraints include strict latency requirements for online serving, hourly retraining for freshness, and addressing exposure bias—the discrepancy between offline training data distribution and online serving data due to auction-based ad exposure. The expected outcome is significant relevance lifts (+8.5% CTR), improved calibration reducing over-prediction from 40% to near zero through iterative calibration with ramped traffic, thereby enhancing both member experience with relevant ads and advertiser ROI while minimizing overcharging risks.

Gousto faced a cold-start problem in their recipe recommendation engine, Rouxcommender, particularly for new customers with limited data and frequently changing weekly menus causing product cold starts. The business challenge was to increase customer retention and trust in recommendations by improving early-stage personalization for subscription users who often rely on the system to choose recipes. Initial solutions like explicit taste preference surveys and item-based collaborative filtering using first order data provided some insights but suffered from sparse data on new recipes and scalability issues with customer ID embeddings. The breakthrough came by redefining customer representation through behavior-based embeddings derived from sequences of ordered recipe embeddings using a bi-encoder deep learning architecture, combining content-based and behavior-based recipe features to alleviate product cold start, enabling fast, synchronous real-time recommendations within 400 ms latency. This approach not only solved cold start for new users but also improved recommendation relevance for existing customers, enhanced diversity across full baskets, reduced training time by fivefold, and opened avenues for integrating additional interaction data and state-of-the-art models, resulting in better customer experience and significant commercial impact.

This use case addresses the challenge of constructing optimal recommendation slates under user time budget constraints, where users sequentially evaluate items with varying relevance and time costs, impacting engagement and abandonment. Targeted at recommender system designers, notably in media streaming contexts like Netflix, the proposed solution models the problem as a Markov Decision Process and applies reinforcement learning (RL) techniques—including temporal difference learning and Q-Learning—to balance item relevance against evaluation cost within a finite time resource. This approach extends traditional bandit-based slate recommenders by incorporating user time budget as a latent state, inferred from interaction data, and aims to maximize user engagement metrics such as play-rate and effective slate size. Simulation results demonstrate that RL methods outperform contextual bandits by better minimizing abandonment through optimized slate construction that fits more relevant items within the user’s time budget, with comparable effectiveness in both on-policy and off-policy learning paradigms.

Peloton’s Personalization team addressed the business problem of delivering diverse, personalized workout class recommendations on connected fitness devices by developing an in-house sequential recommendation model named LSTMNet, aimed at overcoming limitations of the existing AWS Personalize service which lacked interpretability, score outputs, and flexibility for multiple recommendation placements. Intended for Peloton users, the solution leverages user-class consumption sequences over extended periods using a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network that embeds classes and user preference trajectories into dense vector spaces, facilitating ranking by similarity while enabling multi-placement recommendations such as “For Your Usual” and “For Something New.” Constraints included nascent data infrastructure, limited explicit features, and reliance on batch offline predictions refreshed daily, which restricted real-time contextual relevance and led to challenges with newly released classes and cold-start users. Despite achieving comparable or better workout conversion rates than AWS Personalize and providing quantified user-class affinity metrics for improved recommendation diversity, the model struggled with static user representations, scalability for contextual adaptation, popularity bias favoring older classes, and evaluation difficulties due to sequence-dependent data splits. The expected outcome was a scalable, interpretable sequential recommender that advanced Peloton’s early-stage ML ecosystem, enabling personalized daily content while informing directions toward context-aware, online, and hybrid architectures to further improve recommendation relevance and address cold-start problems.

Trivago addresses the explore-exploit dilemma in ranking accommodations by balancing showing well-performing listings (exploitation) versus new, untested ones (exploration) to optimize relevance and conversion in a vast inventory with many unseen options (cold start problem). Users benefit from discovering better accommodations, advertisers gain broader conversion data to optimize bids, and trivago maintains a healthy marketplace by carefully managing this trade-off. Initially, a naive approach optimistic about less-impressed accommodations was used, controlled by a lambda parameter to adjust exploration strength. Subsequently, a model-based approach was developed that predicts performance for low-impression listings using features learned from high-impression ones, enabling smarter exploration. Extensive A/B testing over two quarters revealed that increased exposure to high-quality unexplored inventory improved user value without hurting short-term revenue or advertiser clickshare, and lambda effectively controlled exploration extent. Challenges included ensuring model predictions aligned with exploration objectives and interpreting outputs carefully. The exploration framework is now deployed in production with monitoring tools for continual assessment, combining classical and model-driven strategies to systematically surface promising but previously unseen accommodations in the ranking system.

Walmart addresses the challenge of maintaining multiple domain-specific virtual assistants for voice shopping and store associates by developing a unified multi-task model that jointly performs intent classification and slot filling across these domains. The solution leverages shared retail entities and conversational patterns, combining training data from both assistants, including annotated store live logs enriched via an automated labeling pipeline using multilingual NER models and store-specific heuristics to accurately recognize person and time entities despite linguistic ambiguities and ASR errors. This multi-task learning approach enhances generalization, improves recognition performance for difficult entities, and reduces maintenance and training costs by consolidating models, enabling Walmart to support diverse interaction scenarios with a single robust natural language understanding model.

Grab addresses the business problem of rapidly evolving and diverse fraud patterns across its multi-vertical superapp ecosystem by deploying a scalable, graph-based fraud detection framework intended for fraud analysts and risk teams. Traditional methods like rule engines and decision tree models struggle with unknown fraud cases and require extensive feature engineering and labeled data, which are costly and insufficient for emergent fraud. Leveraging the interconnected entities in Grab’s ecosystem—such as passengers, merchants, devices, and Wi-Fi routers—graph neural networks capture complex spatial correlations indicative of fraud syndicates sharing physical devices and colluding clusters. Using a semi-supervised Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN) trained on large graphs with sparse labels, the system propagates information along graph neighborhoods to produce fraud probability scores with high accuracy and robustness against unknown fraud, minimizing dependency on extensive labeling. This approach also benefits from enhanced explainability via graph visualization of dense, anomalous clusters and maintains effectiveness despite noisy connections and feature initialization challenges, offering a sustainable, real-time adaptable solution that anticipates fraud before occurrence.

The business problem addressed is recommending relevant posts to users in Fishbowl, a professional anonymous networking platform, where explicit negative feedback and rich clickstream data are lacking; intended users are the platform’s working professionals engaging in industry-specific “bowls” or feeds. The proposed solution leverages semantic retrieval via learned embeddings that represent posts and users by combining multiple textual features—post text, company, job title, location, feed name, and feed description—using transfer learning with fine-tuned pre-trained NLP models like GloVe and BERT, supplemented by neural network approaches including Siamese networks and Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) trained with contrastive triplet loss to capture user-post affinity and collaborative signals. Key data elements include user-post interaction data (likes), post popularity metrics (reactions, comments, shares), and textual metadata, while constraints involve limited labeled negatives and the need for generalization to new users/posts. Expected outcomes are improved recommendation precision and recall by capturing nuanced semantic and collaborative similarities, with dimensionality reduction (PCA) enhancing embedding quality and simpler model architectures mitigating overfitting, thereby providing effective semantic retrieval-based personalized ranking in scenarios with sparse implicit feedback.

Glassdoor's Fishbowl platform faces the challenge of recommending relevant anonymous workplace-related posts ("bowls") to users from a vast and growing corpus, without explicit click data to train supervised models. The intended users are active Fishbowl community members who subscribe to bowls and seek personalized content. To address the recommendation problem, the solution employs unsupervised embedding techniques, specifically Doc2Vec models, to convert post texts into numerical vectors capturing semantic similarity; user embeddings are formed by averaging vectors of posts they liked. To enhance personalization beyond content similarity, collaborative filtering is incorporated via graph-based embeddings where user and post IDs form nodes connected by like interactions, and embeddings are learned through breadth-first search contexts within the user-post interaction graph. The combination of content and graph embeddings enables ranking candidate posts per user by cosine similarity scores to yield personalized recommendations from subscribed bowls. Key constraints include the absence of explicit negative engagement signals and the dynamic, rapidly evolving graph of posts and users, which complicates real-time embedding for new entities. The expected outcome is improved ranking and surfacing of relevant posts to enhance user engagement and experience despite limited labeled data.

Dailymotion reengineered its mobile video recommendation system to deliver a personalized, diverse, and explainable home feed that addresses distinct mobile user behaviors and logged-in usage, aiming to enhance user engagement through relevancy and content novelty. The solution employs a simple, rapidly iterated two-stage pipeline comprising candidate retrieval from user interest-stratified groups and ranking via an ensemble of machine-learned rankers that balance freshness, view quality metrics, and format suitability, while incorporating an exploration component to surface less-seen videos and avoid content repetition. Challenges include lack of historical user interaction data and interest imbalance in video supply, mitigated by onboarding interest selection and stratified sampling to ensure diversity. The recommender optimizes for robust engagement metrics like median watch time to favor quality content over clickbait, fostering user retention and satisfaction. Future plans involve deeper personalization using comprehensive user behavior signals to further refine recommendations.

LinkedIn addressed the challenge sales teams faced in efficiently identifying customer accounts at risk of churn or with upsell potential by developing Project Account Prioritizer, an ML-driven system leveraging historical purchases, product usage, hiring trends, and firmographics to score and prioritize accounts for renewals and targeted product recommendations. To increase adoption and trust in the predictions, they integrated CrystalCandle, an explainable AI tool that translates complex model outputs into user-friendly narratives highlighting key features influencing scores, facilitating deeper insights and alignment with sales domain knowledge. This combined solution, embedded within sales platforms like Microsoft Dynamics’ MyBook, enhanced sales efficiency by reducing research time and improving outreach accuracy, resulting in an 8% lift in renewal incremental growth. The system manages complex data labeling across overlapping renewal periods and generates advanced time-series features to predict churn/upsell ahead of actual contract renewals, while employing model interpretation methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME) refined by feature clustering and narrative templating to present actionable explanations tailored for non-technical sales users.

This use case addresses real-time fraud detection in large-scale streaming services plagued by content, service, and account fraud exploiting device and streaming restrictions. Intended for security teams at streaming platforms, the solution combines domain expert-driven heuristics for initial data labeling with supervised and semi-supervised machine learning anomaly detection models, including deep autoencoders and various classifiers, to capture deviations from typical streaming behavior. Leveraging features such as distinct device counts, DRM types, license acquisition rates, and error frequencies, the system uses imbalanced data treatments like SMOTE to enhance detection accuracy. The outcome is an effective, scalable fraud detection framework that automatically identifies suspicious activities, improves precision beyond rule-based methods, and supports multi-label classification of fraud categories to safeguard digital content licensing and enforce platform policies.

PayPal addresses the business challenge of prioritizing sales pipeline opportunities for sales representatives who have limited daily resources by developing a lightweight two-layer ensemble classifier framework for progressive prediction. The intended users are sales teams needing dynamic, timely guidance on which opportunities to focus on each day as new data—such as opportunity age, pipeline stage, and contact attempts—are updated frequently. The solution first applies a Gradient Boosting Machine binary classifier on static features available at opportunity creation to generate an initial propensity score, which is then fed into a logistic regression second layer alongside dynamic features to update the likelihood of closing the opportunity on each run day. This separation of static and dynamic data allows efficient computation and better captures the evolving context, resulting in improved predictive performance over classic static models in prioritizing pipeline opportunities, thereby enabling more effective sales planning and resource allocation.

Gousto addresses the business challenge of customer churn in the meal delivery sector by employing a machine learning solution designed for the Activate Tribe, whose focus is customer retention and satisfaction. The data science team developed a binary classification churn model leveraging over 300 behavioral features—such as order frequency and subscription pauses—processed through a gradient boosted tree algorithm to predict which customers are likely to stop ordering within four weeks. This model outputs churn probabilities interpreted with SHAP values for feature importance insights and is integrated into a Sisense business intelligence dashboard that enables marketing personnel without algorithmic expertise to monitor and analyze churn risks in real time. By adjusting prediction thresholds between precision and recall, the marketing and finance teams tailor timely intervention strategies like promotions or notifications to individual customers, aiming to reduce churn, optimize promotional efforts, and thus improve customer retention, satisfaction, and company profitability.

Grammarly addresses the challenge of grammatical error correction (GEC) for writers who seek reliable editing to avoid damaging communication through grammar, spelling, and punctuation mistakes. The intended users are those sending important writing, who need consistent, contextually accurate suggestions. The solution combines multiple AI techniques, including a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model that rewrites error-ridden text, a sequence tagging system that identifies and corrects specific errors, and pattern-based linguistic rules curated by expert linguists to detect and rectify mistakes. The system balances precision and recall by leveraging curated evaluation datasets and user interaction data to optimize suggestion quality and relevance. Constraints include the evolving norms of language use, ambiguity in correct corrections, and the need for high speed, reliability, and user engagement. The expected outcome is a state-of-the-art, trust-building GEC system that continuously improves and personalizes grammar suggestions, enhancing user communication effectiveness.

Instacart addresses the challenge of helping eCommerce users efficiently find and explore products by deploying a machine learning-driven Autocomplete system in its search feature, aimed at shoppers seeking to fill their carts effortlessly. Intended for Instacart customers across various retailers with differing catalogs, the solution leverages a vast dataset of 11.3 million products and past search logs to generate query suggestions while filtering out irrelevant or inappropriate terms and handling misspellings via fuzzy matching. Semantic deduplication using pretrained search embeddings reduces redundant suggestions, enhancing user experience. To overcome cold-start problems for new or low-traffic retailers, the system uses a shared standardized product catalog to augment query suggestions. A multi-objective ranking model combines engagement data and add-to-cart likelihood to optimize suggestion relevance and conversion rates. This approach results in measurable improvements like increased autocomplete engagement, shorter prefix lengths, larger basket sizes, and higher gross transaction values, ultimately transforming Autocomplete into a strategic tool that guides customer search behavior, improves product discoverability, and enhances cart building.

Meta addressed Instagram's challenge of notification overload by combining causal inference and machine learning to personalize daily digest push notifications. Traditional click-through rate (CTR) models highlighted potential notification engagement but failed to recognize highly active users who would organically view stories without notifications, leading to unnecessary messaging. To optimize notification sending under a fixed budget, the team framed it as a causal problem estimating the incremental impact of sending versus dropping notifications for each user. They conducted randomized experiments and developed neural network uplift models to predict these effects in real-time, dynamically selecting notifications for users who would most benefit. By stabilizing send rates via online quantile normalization, this approach substantially reduced notification volume without reducing user engagement, enhancing user experience while conserving resources.

eBay addresses the challenge of effectively recommending Promoted Listings Standard (PLS) items, which are paid ads charged on sale, by developing a multi-stage machine learning ranking system that ranks similar sponsored items shown on a View Item (VI) page. The target users are online shoppers browsing item details, where the system first recalls relevant PLS candidates related to the seed item, then applies a gradient boosted tree ranker trained on multi-relevance feedback signals—which include not just purchase (the highest relevance) but also intermediate user actions such as Buy It Now, Add to Cart, Make Offer, and Add to Watchlist—weighted to capture varying purchase intent intensity. Historical interaction data and context features like product category and personalization inform the model, which balances item relevance with seller ad-rates to optimize conversion and seller velocity. Using carefully tuned sample weights in the loss function enables the model to distinguish nuanced user engagement levels beyond binary purchase data, leading to improved offline metrics and A/B tests showing increased purchase counts and ad revenue, thereby enhancing shopping experience and maximizing conversion in eBay’s complex marketplace.

Spotify addressed the limitation of traditional term-based search for podcast episodes, which struggled with natural language variation and exact word matches, by implementing Natural Language Search leveraging semantic retrieval through Dense Retrieval. Targeting podcast listeners, the solution uses a shared embedding space generated by fine-tuned Universal Sentence Encoder CMLM Transformer models to produce vectors representing queries and episode metadata (title, description, show info). Training data included past successful search pairs, query reformulations, synthetic queries, and curated semantic queries, while in-batch negatives and margin loss techniques enhanced learning. Indexed episode vectors are served by Vespa’s Approximate Nearest Neighbor search for low-latency retrieval, complemented by online query vector encoding via GPU-accelerated Google Cloud Vertex AI. Integrated as an additional retrieval source alongside Elasticsearch, the system feeds a final-stage ranking model enriched with cosine similarity features, yielding a significant increase in podcast engagement by better capturing semantic relevance beyond exact matches.

LinkedIn addresses the challenge of improving AI model performance across heterogeneous and related tasks such as job recommendation, job search, and recruiter search by implementing a multitask learning framework that enables simultaneous training on multiple tasks with shared and task-specific components. This framework accommodates differences in label distributions, input features, and model architectures by unifying data schemas, relaxing input constraints, and allowing developers to specify shared and task-specific model parts. Training can be conducted via joint or iterative approaches, balancing task losses and hyperparameters dynamically. Applied to cross-domain skill extraction from job postings and resumes using multilingual and entity embeddings, and to cross-domain member-company affinity learning for recruiter search by co-training embeddings representing recruiter-candidate affinity, multitask learning has significantly improved key business metrics such as user engagement, click-through rates, InMail acceptances, and confirmed hires, demonstrating enhanced model generalization and relevance across LinkedIn’s products.

The New York Times addresses the business problem of optimizing its paywall to maximize subscriptions while maintaining user engagement with content, targeting registered users whose meter limits dictate article access before subscription prompts. Using first-party engagement data without demographic biases, the company employs a causal machine learning approach called the Dynamic Meter, which is a prescriptive model trained on randomized controlled trial data to account for the counterfactual "missing data" problem inherent in treatment effect estimation. The model simultaneously optimizes two competing key performance indicators—subscription conversion rates and reader engagement—through a weighted objective function, allowing dynamic personalized meter limits that balance trade-offs between generating subscriptions and sustaining readership. Backtesting via inverse probability weighting and Pareto front analysis enables tuning the friction parameter controlling this balance, ensuring the paywall strategy adapts optimally to business goals while improving overall engagement and subscription outcomes compared to a static or random policy.

Wayfair addresses the challenge of helping millions of customers discover niche "long tail" furniture products by employing aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) to extract fine-grained sentiments about specific product features from customer reviews. Intended for shoppers and site curators, their solution leverages a BERT-based transformer model combined with a self-attention network to simultaneously identify relevant product aspects—such as "comfort" or "delivery"—and their associated sentiments in a single step, improving accuracy and relevance over traditional two-step methods. The approach requires carefully refined labeling guidelines to mitigate subjectivity in defining important aspects, ensuring that the model highlights sentiment-laden features customers truly care about. This enables automated generation of specialized marketing pages and offers potential for enhanced product filtering by sentiment-tagged attributes, ultimately aiming to improve product discovery and customer satisfaction in Wayfair’s vast catalog.

Mercado Libre addresses the challenge of missing package dimensions, crucial for accurate shipping cost prediction and fulfillment center capacity planning, by developing a machine-learning solution targeting sellers and logistics operators. The solution leverages a semantic similarity model that predicts an item's weight, height, width, and length based on metadata fields—title, category, brand, and model—using a pipeline with NLP preprocessing, FastText embeddings, and a K approximate Nearest Neighbors (KNN) regression approach. The heterogeneous source data undergo an ETL process to align item metadata with shipment dimensions, creating training, development, and test datasets normalized for consistent vector representations. During prediction, the model retrieves the nearest neighbors from an Annoy index and filters them by a distance threshold, estimating dimensions via median aggregation of neighbors' known values. This model, integrated into product listings and packaging calculators, delivers real-time dimension predictions at high volume (up to 29 million/day with 5ms latency), enhancing cost forecasts, packaging efficiency, and overall user experience in Mercado Libre's shipping ecosystem.

Google Docs addresses the challenge faced by document writers and readers in managing large volumes of text by offering auto-generated, concise 1-2 sentence summaries of documents to help prioritize and navigate content efficiently. Leveraging advances in abstractive summarization through sequence-to-sequence machine learning models based on Transformer architectures and the Pegasus model’s novel Gap Sentence Prediction pre-training, the system achieves high-quality natural language summaries with minimal supervised fine-tuning on carefully curated, consistent datasets. To meet production deployment constraints, knowledge distillation transforms the large Transformer model into a more efficient hybrid of Transformer encoder and RNN decoder that improves latency and reduces resource usage, further accelerated by TPU serving. This ML-driven semantic retrieval and generation solution enhances workplace written communication by assisting users with document comprehension and summary creation while preserving writer control over suggested summaries, primarily benefiting Google Workspace business customers.

Instacart addresses the challenge of improving search relevance across a vast product catalog of over one billion items by developing ITEMS (Instacart Transformer-based Embedding Model for Search), a semantic retrieval system using a bi-encoder architecture to independently encode search queries and product data into a shared embedding space. Intended for shoppers seeking highly relevant, personalized product results, ITEMS leverages fine-tuned deep learning with positive (query, product) pairs mined from search logs (customer conversions) and in-batch negatives for irrelevant pairs, augmented by synthetic queries and multi-task learning using rich product metadata to enhance coverage and model stability. The model overcomes noisy e-commerce signals by cascading training with a large, noisier dataset followed by fine-tuning on higher-quality data, enabling robust semantic matching beyond keyword and category heuristics. Deploying precomputed embeddings in an approximate nearest neighbor search with a hybrid caching strategy allows sub-8ms retrieval latency, which significantly improves search metrics such as mean reciprocal rank and cart additions per search. ITEMS also supports semantic deduplication to enhance result diversity, ultimately delivering a more efficient, relevant search experience that better captures customer intent and preferences.

Google Workspace addresses information overload in hybrid work environments by providing abstractive conversation summaries in Google Chat Spaces, aimed at business users needing quick catch-up on unread messages. Leveraging the Pegasus model fine-tuned on ForumSum—a high-quality dataset of multi-speaker internet forum conversations with human-written summaries—the solution generates concise, fluent digests of chat threads, highlighting key topics and facilitating navigation to relevant discussions. To optimize performance for real-time use, Pegasus is distilled into a hybrid transformer encoder and RNN decoder, reducing latency and memory use, while summaries are pre-generated and cached upon message updates. Despite challenges like misattribution and misrepresentation in generated summaries, this semantic retrieval application enhances productivity by summarizing complex conversational data with improved accuracy and fluency.

DoorDash faced the business challenge of expanding its product search beyond food delivery to include multiple new verticals like groceries, alcohol, and pet food, requiring a more scalable, domain-agnostic search system. Intended users are consumers seeking diverse products across these categories, and the solution involved rebuilding the search infrastructure with active/nextgen indexing to accelerate indexing speed, federated search for vertical-agnostic result retrieval and blending, and exploring advanced storage engines beyond ElasticSearch for performance and cost efficiency. Managing the semantic complexity of disparate product taxonomies, DoorDash bootstrapped new domain labels through human annotations combined with machine learning models, employing natural language processing (NLP) methods such as part-of-speech tagging to enrich query understanding. To improve relevance, learning-to-rank models—starting with pointwise ranking based on diverse query, lexical, store, and user interaction features—were developed and integrated with a rigorous search evaluation framework leveraging both implicit engagement signals and human-in-the-loop feedback, further enhanced by personalization for non-branded search queries. This holistic approach, incorporating scalable indexing, domain-aware semantic labeling, NLP enrichment, and ML-driven ranking, aimed at delivering fresh, relevant, and personalized search results across all DoorDash verticals, ultimately boosting consumer engagement and conversion metrics.

Wayfair addresses the business problem of providing efficient, 24/7 customer service through a Virtual Assistant (VA) that uses text-based intent prediction to automate support and reduce resolution times by identifying customer intent and relevant product/order information. Intended for customers interacting via chat, the solution involved creating a detailed hierarchical intent taxonomy with 11 broad categories and 70 subcategories derived from analyzing 10,000 chats, followed by manual labeling of approximately 200,000 chat utterances for model training. Employing fine-tuned BERT and later a faster distilBERT model, the approach framed intent prediction as a multi-label, multi-class classification task, achieving over 90% accuracy and inference times below 100 ms to ensure seamless conversations. Backend infrastructure was custom-built (HaloAI) for scalability and rapid iteration, addressing challenges such as shifting intent distributions and shorter utterance lengths in bot interactions compared to live chats. The expected outcome includes improved customer engagement, automated resolution of inquiries, and ongoing enhancements like multilingual support and entity recognition to further personalize and streamline the customer experience.

Wayfair's Nightingale is a scalable family of machine learning models designed to optimize daily sales email dispatch to millions of customers by predicting the probabilities of purchase, unsubscription, or no action, leveraging over 500 selected customer interaction features. The business problem addresses balancing customer engagement and unsubscribe costs, scaling model retraining efficiently across regions and brands, and countering model performance decay using an automated pipeline integrated with the Mercury feature platform. Nightingale combines predicted action probabilities with estimated gross revenue stability and unsubscribe costs to generate a net value score, informing email sending frequency decisions mapped through business-logic-defined bins. The solution involves automated retraining triggered by performance monitoring, unbiased data collection from randomized email frequencies, and modular pipeline components supporting extensibility to new models and data sources. The model exhibits improved AUC scores (~0.8 for purchase/null and ~0.7 for unsubscribe) and demonstrated in A/B tests a 7% reduction in unsubscribe rates without affecting revenue or engagement. Challenges remain in integrating multiple ML models cost-effectively and automating threshold selection for send decisions, with future plans to incorporate reinforcement learning and richer feature embeddings to enhance personalization while managing system complexity.

Nextdoor addresses the business challenge of reducing uncivil and abusive interactions on its neighborhood social platform by leveraging machine learning for early detection and intervention in contentious conversation threads to foster kindness and constructive dialogue among neighbors. Intended users include neighbors engaged in discussions, community moderators, and neighborhood staff. The solution employs a predictive thread model that uses a combination of linguistic embeddings (primarily leveraging multilingual BERT for cross-lingual applicability), comment text, conversation structure (mentions, reply hierarchy, sequential order), and additional behavioral features to anticipate when threads may escalate into abusive exchanges, allowing for proactive nudges such as Kindness and Constructive Conversations Reminders and comment notification suppression. Training data relies on user-reported content to label contentious interactions, managing class imbalance through strategic sampling, and internationalization adapts the model to multiple languages using aligned multilingual embeddings for scalability across regions. Expected outcomes include a significant reduction in abusive comments by interrupting negative feedback loops common in contentious comment threads, with model performance demonstrating strong predictive accuracy (AUC > 0.83) and practical effectiveness in live deployment to support community moderation and enhance neighborly engagement globally.

The Guardian, in collaboration with Daily Maverick and Follow the Money during the 2022 JournalismAI fellowship, addressed the business problem of efficiently identifying "bad actors" within large, complex data leaks to aid investigative journalists. Targeting newsroom professionals, they developed an AI-powered entity linking pipeline to automatically disambiguate named entities—such as persons sharing surnames—by linking mentions in text to unique identifiers from combined databases (LittleSis and Open Sanctions), overcoming challenges like inconsistent data formatting, duplicate entries, and limited training examples for ambiguous or single-name entities. Using NLP tools spaCy and Prodigy, with extensive annotated data from Guardian articles, the solution aimed to reduce manual labor in entity recognition and connection mapping, although model performance revealed needs for more training data and improved handling of ambiguous cases. Expected outcomes include streamlined identification of individuals and organizations of interest in document collections, enhanced investigative journalism workflows, and the eventual expansion of the model to map complex relational graphs between entities.

Snapchat’s ad ranking system addresses the business problem of serving the most relevant ads from millions of options to users in real time while preserving user privacy and experience, benefiting both advertisers and Snapchatters. Intended users include Snapchat’s ad engineers and advertisers. The solution leverages a multi-stage pipeline combining eligibility filtering, lightweight candidate generation, and heavy deep learning models that predict conversion probabilities and organic utility for ads, followed by a real-time auction integrating bids and budgets. Key data challenges include handling massive-scale input (billions of training examples, trillions of daily predictions), fast-changing ad inventory, delayed and repeated conversion events, auction-induced selection bias, and calibration requirements to ensure predicted conversions align with actual outcomes. The system employs state-of-the-art deep learning architectures such as multi-task MMoE and PLE models, optimized distributed training (including TPU usage), continuous incremental updates to adapt to delayed feedback, and an internal platform for streamlined feature engineering and model management. Online evaluation uses a budget-split A/B testing framework to measure business impact without cross-budget bias, while extensive real-time monitoring ensures model and feature stability amid high churn and scale. This comprehensive ML pipeline enables dynamic, calibrated, low-latency ad ranking at Snapchat’s scale, maximizing conversion predictions and advertiser value while maintaining cost and latency constraints.

The business problem involves accurately tagging restaurants with cuisine labels on a large food delivery platform to enhance customer search and discovery, complicated by the subjective and culturally dependent definitions of cuisines and the presence of multi-cultural menus. The intended users are customers searching for specific cuisines and internal labeling specialists who validate the model outputs. The proposed solution combines user behavior analysis—using keyword-driven search clicks to infer cuisine interest—and a semi-supervised approach leveraging fastText embeddings of menu items to measure cosine similarity between restaurants, thereby propagating cuisine labels to unlabelled cases. Constraints include reliance on a predefined list of cuisines, ambiguity in fusion menus, and potential false positives from similar dish names. The expected outcome is a scalable, interpretable model with improved accuracy and efficiency over manual labeling, which integrates customer context to better reflect local culinary perspectives and reduces subjective label inconsistencies while enabling confident production deployment.

Lyft addresses the business problem of optimizing rideshare pricing to balance supply and demand, ensure fairness and reliability, and maintain competitiveness within a dynamic marketplace influenced by driver availability and rider demand. Intended users include riders seeking consistent and fair prices and drivers whose platform participation affects pricing. The solution comprises a three-layered system: pricing orchestration (a robust engineering platform ensuring price stability and traceability using technologies like Flink, TensorFlow, and reinforcement learning), pricing operations (strategic and tactical guidance aligning with business objectives), and algorithmic pricing (a large-scale real-time pricing engine employing causal inference, machine learning, and reinforcement learning that performs offline training, online learning, and real-time evaluation). Key data inputs include ride characteristics, market signals, and driver activity, with constraints such as compliance with GDPR/CCPA and the complex non-linear demand response to pricing. The expected outcome is the continuous generation of fair, reliable, and competitive prices that improve marketplace efficiency, rider conversion, and overall long-term passenger value through adaptive, data-driven decision-making in a volatile transportation market.

LinkedIn Talent Solutions addresses the challenge of enhancing job matching for active job seekers by leveraging members' recent job-seeking activities to better personalize recommendations beyond static profile data.
