Users—including job seekers engaging with jobs via actions such as apply, save, or dismiss—generate sequences of job interactions characterized by low-dimensional job embeddings and timestamps. Rather than traditional sparse, high-dimensional skill aggregation or simple averaging, LinkedIn developed a machine-learned embedding approach: initially using unweighted averages, then incorporating recency through geometrically decaying weighted averages, and finally employing sequence-based deep learning models like CNNs to capture complex temporal and action-type interactions within a member's activity sequence. Training involved predicting subsequent member actions to optimize embedding quality despite skewed positive/negative label distributions, addressed via negative sampling and sliding window techniques. The precomputed member activity embeddings are updated frequently and integrated into job recommendation systems such as JYMBII, resulting in significant improvements—including over 10% increase in job applications and 5% in hires—while reducing feature storage by threefold. Future work aims to refine modeling with session-based approaches, expand to course recommendations, incorporate broader member behaviors, and transition to real-time embedding updates for more responsive personalization.

The business problem addressed is optimizing item rankings on interactive systems like homepages or search results to enhance user engagement despite noisy and implicit user feedback, which often leads traditional supervised learning models to suboptimal recommendations due to limited exploration. Intended users include recommendation system designers and data scientists working with large candidate item sets where full feedback on all items is unavailable. The proposed solution employs cascade bandits, a structured contextual bandit approach leveraging the cascade click model that assumes users scan ranked lists sequentially and click on the first attractive item, enabling learning of item attractiveness probabilities while accounting for position bias. The method uses Thompson sampling within the CascadeLinTS algorithm to balance exploration and exploitation efficiently by modeling attraction probabilities as a linear function of item features and context, allowing for scalable learning despite combinatorial ranking spaces. The approach harnesses click data to iteratively update beliefs about item relevance, resulting in improved ranking quality and reduced regret compared to greedy strategies that lack exploration, ultimately surfacing more relevant and personalized item rankings for users.

Expedia Group addresses the business problem of efficiently routing thousands of daily customer feedback messages to appropriate teams without the availability of large labeled datasets for supervised training. Intended users include internal customer service teams responsible for handling diverse traveler feedback related to flights, hotels, and car rentals. The proposed solution leverages unsupervised learning by employing heuristic algorithms that utilize pre-trained high-dimensional word embeddings from models like GloVe to measure semantic distances between feedback keywords and category labels, enabling multi-label classification without manual annotation. Constraints involve tuning distance thresholds per category to optimize classification accuracy, while preprocessing cleans feedback text. The expected outcome is improved automated categorization of unstructured customer feedback, facilitating faster and more accurate team assignments to enhance traveler satisfaction and operational efficiency.

Netflix addresses the business challenge of quantifying the causal impact of product changes and content localization on member engagement and satisfaction by leveraging causal inference techniques tailored for different contexts. Intended users include data scientists, product teams, and content strategists aiming to optimize recommendations, localization efforts, and subscriber value. The proposed solutions encompass AB testing, quasi-experimental designs like difference-in-differences, double machine learning to control confounders, synthetic control methods for simulating counterfactual scenarios, and holdback experiments to measure long-term feature effects. Additionally, Netflix integrates causal methods into recommendation systems through a Causal Ranker framework to move beyond correlational models toward causally informed personalization. Key data challenges include avoiding technical and operational issues in large-scale experiments and managing incomplete data for off-platform subscriber behavior. Expected outcomes include more accurate estimations of incremental value from localization and features, improved recommendation relevance, optimized acquisition and retention policies based on incremental lifetime value, and enhanced decision-making confidence that collectively contribute to delivering more engaging and personalized member experiences worldwide.

Instacart faces the challenge of personalizing product recommendations for users who are simultaneously learning and evolving their preferences during interaction, complicating traditional recommendation approaches. The intended users are shoppers on Instacart whose preferences update as they accept or reject recommended item categories, individual items, or algorithms presented as arms in a multi-armed bandit framework. The proposed solution, the best arm identification under revealed preference (BAIR) algorithm, models user interaction as sequential and incorporates the user's binary accept/reject feedback while assuming users update their confidence intervals on rewards rationally. BAIR operates in two phases: a cautious "sweeping" phase presenting all arms to collect safe acceptances while minimizing early rejections, followed by an "elimination" phase that progressively removes suboptimal arms to identify the best recommendation. This approach accommodates user exploration and evolving preferences, unlike classical bandit methods that treat user feedback as stationary or black-box, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency in surfacing optimal recommendations. By leveraging this realistic user learning model and handling uncertainty in early feedback, BAIR enables Instacart to iteratively deliver high-quality personalized recommendations as users refine their tastes, ensuring an enhanced, adaptive shopping experience.

DoorDash faced the challenge of ensuring customers receive acceptable substitutions when ordered items, especially in new verticals like grocery with extensive SKUs and inventory volatility; their intended users are delivery drivers ("Dashers") and customers who need seamless substitutions without real-time communication. To solve this, DoorDash evolved their substitution recommendation system from an initial unsupervised TF-IDF cosine similarity model leveraging item metadata and taxonomy heuristics, to a supervised LightGBM binary classifier informed by customer "thumbs-up/down" feedback, and ultimately to a deep learning recommendation model using semantic item embeddings trained on user search behaviors. This progression enabled more contextually relevant and quantity-aware substitutes, improving coverage and customer approval rates while reducing the friction of manual substitutions. Constraints included sparse labeled data initially and the need to handle items with limited purchase history. The outcome was improved customer satisfaction, fewer refunds, and increased merchant sales, with ongoing plans to incorporate richer item metadata, image embeddings, and personalization to address complex categories like produce and meat.

DoorDash addresses the challenge of personalized homepage recommendations balancing known user preferences (exploitation) and introducing new options (exploration) to enhance user engagement and merchant fairness. Targeting consumers browsing the limited homepage real estate consisting of mixed entities—restaurants, store carousels, and items—DoorDash developed a universal ranker (UR), a deep-learning learn-to-rank model integrating heterogeneous entity types by representing high-level entities as ordered sequences of lower-level ones, leveraging features spanning entity attributes, consumer profiles, historical engagement, and contextual signals. To avoid filter bubbles and adapt to changing preferences, they incorporate exploration through an upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm from reinforcement learning, which quantifies uncertainty in expected conversion probabilities (pConv) to smartly trade off recommending familiar favorites and novel options. This composite model ranks entities by combining UR’s predicted conversion likelihood and exploration-driven uncertainty, refreshed daily with consumer interaction data, enabling dynamic and calibrated homepage rankings that improve conversion rates, consumer discovery, and marketplace fairness. Their integrated ranking framework applies these ML models progressively across retrieval and ranking stages, validated by online experiments demonstrating increased user engagement and diversified merchant exposure, with future plans to personalize exploration coefficients and extend exploration strategies deeper into recommendation pipelines.

Yelp addressed the challenge of improving personalized user-to-business recommendations, especially for tail users with sparse interaction data, by transitioning from a matrix factorization collaborative filtering approach to a supervised hybrid model integrating both interaction-based and content-based features. Their solution combined matrix factorization scores with engineered features such as business categories, user metadata, and a novel text-based similarity metric derived from Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings of reviews, optimized using XGBoost's LambdaMART with objectives based on Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG). The hybrid model effectively handled cold-start problems and scaled predictions by incorporating recall steps constrained by user location and product-specific criteria. Evaluations demonstrated significant improvements in recommendation quality (doubling NDCG over popularity baselines and 5-14% gains over matrix factorization) with content signals influencing tail users more and collaborative signals benefiting head users, validating the hybrid approach’s nuanced use of diverse features to enhance recommendation performance across user segments.

The business problem addressed is predicting service time—the period drivers spend parking, re-stacking, scanning orders, and delivering groceries—to improve delivery route planning and operational efficiency. Intended users include logistics planners and delivery drivers in Oda’s grocery delivery service. The solution involves developing a machine learning model using gradient boosting (lightgbm) trained on two years of delivery data featuring order size, geographic area, and customer-specific attributes such as floor and elevator availability. This model replaced a manual Business logic model, yielding a 23% reduction in mean absolute error (MAE) for service time predictions and about 30 seconds better accuracy per stop when tested in a representative region. Despite the improved stop-level predictions, overall route delivery precision improved only modestly, likely because errors in individual stop estimates offset each other over multi-stop routes. Constraints include messy, unpredictable road data and environmental factors like weather, which currently require manual adjustments. The expected outcome is an iterative, scalable system with reduced need for manual oversight and enhanced operational insights, with plans to better filter training data and incorporate dynamic features to adapt to environmental drift.

Grammarly addresses the challenge of delivering accurate and relevant text correction suggestions in its Editor, used by millions, by employing an extensible operational transformation (OT) protocol based on the Delta format to represent both user edits and suggestions uniformly. The system manages suggestions—including complex multi-word or multi-paragraph edits—by storing them in a Suggestions Repository and updating them in real-time using a Delta Manager that continuously rebases suggestion Deltas to align with ongoing user text changes, ensuring suggestions remain correctly targeted and contextually relevant without backend latency. Applying suggestions involves composing these Deltas with the current text state, and to maintain UI responsiveness when accepting multiple suggestions simultaneously, Grammarly developers devised an algorithm that rebases and composes all suggestion Deltas into one before updating the text, preventing interface freezes and maintaining text integrity. This carefully orchestrated architecture balances computational complexity with user experience to support sophisticated semantic retrieval and correction tasks within a cloud-based collaborative text editor.

Airbnb addressed the business challenge of inspiring travelers beyond conventional search by creating curated “categories” of unique listings defined by location, activity, home type, or amenity; this helps users discover distinctive stays off popular paths. The intended users are travelers seeking inspirational browsing rather than fixed-destination searches. The solution combines rule-based candidate generation using listing features and points of interest with a human-in-the-loop system for verifying categories, selecting representative photos, and rating photo quality. Human-labeled data then trains binary classification ML models for scalable listing categorization with precision-recall thresholds guiding automated and manual review to balance accuracy and coverage. Additional ML models estimate listing quality tiers and select cover images. Two novel ranking algorithms optimize category and listing order based on user context, inventory, and quality. This integrated human and ML workflow enables dynamic, personalized semantic retrieval of Airbnb's extensive listings, enhancing discovery and booking through meaningful category groupings.

Lyft faces the business problem of efficiently managing its marketplace by optimizing financial incentives for drivers and riders to maintain affordable rides and low ETAs amid changing market conditions, with intended users being internal product-focused teams responsible for driver bonuses, rider coupons, and pricing. The proposed solution is a large-scale causal forecasting system that models key business metrics (e.g., ride counts, revenue) as functions of controllable policy variables (e.g., spending budgets), using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to encode causal relationships validated by experimental data, which distinguishes it from correlational forecasting. Important data considerations include integrating empirical cost curves derived from experiments (such as driver incentive budgets versus driver hours) to ensure models adhere to realistic causal effects, avoiding misleading correlations. The expected outcome is a comprehensive and causally valid predictive model that enables accurate forecasting and optimization of policy decisions—supporting scenario planning and capital allocation—to maximize business objectives under constraints like revenue per ride.

Pinterest addresses the business challenge of enhancing user engagement on its Homefeed, a critical platform surface for content discovery, by targeting personalized pin recommendations. The intended users are Pinterest pinners, including new, casual, and resurrected users. The solution integrates a real-time user action sequence feature, processed by a transformer encoder within their Pinnability ranking model, complementing long-term user embeddings like PinnerSAGE. This approach models short-term user interests by consuming the latest 100 user actions, including pin embeddings, action types, and timestamps, enabling quicker model responsiveness and end-to-end optimization for relevance prediction. Key constraints involve managing signal latency, avoiding data leakage, and overcoming the increased computational complexity by shifting from CPU to GPU serving. Frequent model retraining (biweekly) is crucial to counteract engagement rate decay due to real-time sensitivity. Offline and online evaluations demonstrate significant improvements, notably a 6–11% increase in repin volume and a reduction in hide rates, with a positive feedback loop further amplifying engagement gains post-deployment. This use of transformer architectures for real-time sequence modeling substantially boosts personalized recommendation quality on Pinterest’s Homefeed.

Lyft addresses the complex business problem of making causally valid forecasts to optimize decisions affecting metrics like rides, ETA, and profitability, targeting data scientists and business users involved in operational and strategic planning. Their solution extends PyTorch into a Causal Forecasting System featuring a novel data structure called IndexTensors—PyTorch tensors indexed like Pandas for aligned, differentiable operations—and modular, composable causal models organized as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). These models integrate experimental and observational data to predict outcomes and optimize high-dimensional decision variables, such as driver incentives, under constraints. Key challenges include enabling parallel model development, managing aggregations for scalability, providing fast iteration cycles, and evaluating model quality via causal validity and predictive accuracy metrics like Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE). The system supports retrospective analysis and decision optimization through autograd-enabled gradient methods, ultimately delivering automated or human-in-the-loop recommendations that improve Lyft’s marketplace performance while quantifying decision "regret" to guide iterative improvements.

Twitter addresses the business problem of personalized account recommendations (Who-To-Follow) by using a two-stage machine learning pipeline comprising candidate generation and ranking to connect users with accounts matching their interests. The intended users are Twitter consumers seeking relevant accounts to follow, especially new users expanding their follow graph. The proposed solution replaces multiple narrow-scope candidate sources with a unified, model-based framework employing a two-tower embedding model—one tower capturing consumption behaviors and the other production behaviors—trained on actual follow relationships. This allows computation of consumer and producer embeddings whose dot product estimates follow probability, enabling retrieval of k-nearest producer embeddings as personalized recommendations. Important data includes behavioral, graph-based, and personalized features fed into the embedding towers, while constraints involve maintaining a scalable and maintainable pipeline. Expected outcomes include improved recommendation relevance, increased user engagement, retirement of legacy heuristics, streamlined maintenance, and the ability to efficiently incorporate new signals for continual model enhancement.

Faire addresses the challenge of delivering personalized, high-quality search rankings to retailers by developing a comprehensive feature store system that unifies and optimizes feature creation, serving, and monitoring for machine learning models. Intended for data scientists and ML engineers, this system integrates both offline batch-computed features—generated daily via SQL in a data warehouse and stored in a global feature registry for visibility and reuse—and real-time computed features drawn from live user interactions and backend services. By consolidating feature definitions and enforcing constraints through Airflow orchestration, they reduce redundancy, ensure data quality, and facilitate scalable online accessibility with low latency through Redis caching. The system supports complex user-item interaction features computed dynamically to avoid combinatorial explosion, and implements a log-and-wait paradigm that captures all features at inference time for straightforward, consistent model training without backfilling. Metadata management and time-series anomaly detection provide robust monitoring to detect feature drift or failures. This feature ecosystem enables efficient retrieval targeted to specific ranking contexts, balancing predictive power and operational simplicity to continually improve Faire’s real-time ranking models.

Amazon Music addresses the challenge of music recommendation lacking context about user mood or company by enabling US customers to converse with Alexa for tailored suggestions. Initially rule-based and semi-scripted, the system evolved into a machine learning-driven conversational recommender that selects optimal follow-up prompts using offline reinforcement learning to maximize prompt usefulness—measured by prompts leading to user-played tracks—based on anonymized dialogue data from 50,000 sessions. This ML model also incorporates individual listening histories to personalize recommendations, improving successful outcomes and reducing conversation length. Offline policy optimization allows safe experimentation with prompt selection and counterfactual analysis, enhancing dialogue policies before deployment. The system offers a fluid conversational experience balancing user and system initiative, with future enhancements targeting sentiment analysis to gauge user engagement and empathy, thereby refining interaction quality to better help users find desired music.

Walmart addresses the business problem of identifying optimal curated product combinations to increase basket size and revenue across its vast product catalog and millions of transactions by developing a scalable, distributed product recommendation engine using basket analysis. Intended for use across diverse departments and divisions, the solution leverages transactional data from e-commerce and in-store purchases, applying filters based on support, price, and gross merchandise value to select relevant products while mitigating bias. Two modeling approaches—FP Growth for frequent pattern mining and a probability-based item pairing method focusing on item co-occurrence—are evaluated, with the probability-based approach preferred due to its computational efficiency and scalability achieved via PySpark distributed processing. The system generates hundreds of thousands of association rules validated over varying timeframes, enabling cross-category product pairing recommendations that reflect customer shopping behavior. The outcome is a more efficient, department-wide recommendation system that balances complexity and scalability, ultimately enhancing personalized marketing, supply chain planning, and promotional bundling, albeit with ongoing efforts to address cold-start challenges for new products.

Walmart addresses the challenge of maintaining half a million diverse refrigeration systems storing perishable goods by forecasting temperature anomalies to reduce malfunctions and optimize maintenance efforts. Using telemetry sensor data collected every 10 minutes on components like compressors, fans, and valves, along with external air temperature forecasts, the solution aggregates data hourly and models temperature over the next 72 hours. Various time series forecasting models, including ARIMAX, BSTS, and Prophet, were evaluated, with Prophet selected for its balance of accuracy, efficiency, and ability to detect change-points indicating sudden temperature trend shifts. Anomalies are detected by comparing forecasts against predefined favorable temperature bands per refrigeration type and prioritized by magnitude and duration, validated through recall against registered malfunctions, achieving 67–84% accuracy depending on historical temperature context. The system is deployed via scalable batch processing with PySpark on Azure Cloud, integrating into Walmart’s cloud-native platform to proactively flag and prioritize refrigeration anomalies for technical teams, ultimately enhancing maintenance efficiency and reducing food spoilage.

The use case addresses the challenge in e-commerce voice ordering systems of recognizing multiple product name entities (MPNER) in a single utterance, which existing solutions like Amazon Alexa fail to handle effectively due to ambiguity, absence of punctuation, and diversity in product names. Target users are customers who want to add multiple items to their shopping cart via voice commands, improving shopping efficiency and experience. The proposed solution is an Entity Transformer (ET) neural network with an encoder-decoder architecture combining transformer layers and a Conditional Random Field (CRF) decoder, leveraging dense embeddings from pre-trained models such as conveRT, BERT, and sparse features like character n-grams. Trained on a large, augmented dataset of about 1 million product entities extracted from natural voice orders, the ET model effectively segments and labels up to 10 product entities per utterance, outperforming non-neural baselines and BERT-based models by 12% on accuracy. This system enables accurate semantic retrieval of multiple product items from noisy ASR transcripts lacking punctuation, enhancing the voice reorder experience in retail environments.

LinkedIn addresses the challenge of estimating causal impacts of product changes when A/B testing is infeasible or costly—such as advertising campaigns or economic shocks—by using observational causal inference through its Ocelot platform. Intended for data scientists and product teams, Ocelot provides a user-friendly web application integrated with automated data pipelines that standardize study setup, covariate selection via an internal feature store, and execution of advanced causal methods including Coarsened Exact Matching, Doubly Robust estimators, Instrumental Variables, Fixed Effects Models, and Bayesian Structured Time Series. By enforcing rigorous design, validation with automated robustness checks like A/A testing, and centralized expert review, Ocelot enables scalable, reliable causal analysis of non-randomized treatments on metrics affecting LinkedIn's 875+ million members, significantly reducing study time from weeks to days and democratizing causal inference across the company to inform product strategy and improve member experiences.

This use case addresses the challenge of accurate product categorization in ecommerce catalogs with thousands of evolving, semantically related categories, where traditional one-hot encoding (OHE) fails to capture class similarities, causing severe classification errors. Intended for data scientists and engineers working on multimodal classification systems, the proposed solution introduces semantic label representations that leverage a-priori semantic information and label smoothing to produce soft targets reflecting inter-class relationships, particularly utilizing CLIP embeddings for category names and combining focal loss with KL divergence loss to train classifiers more effectively on a large, imbalanced dataset of product images and titles. Experimental results on 4,350 product categories across 12 million items demonstrate that semantic-aware label smoothing substantially improves both top-1/top-5 accuracy and the semantic similarity of misclassifications by encouraging the model to make "better" mistakes within semantically close categories, enhancing real-world product navigation and user experience in large taxonomies.

Coupang addresses the business problem of duplicate product listings in its online marketplace, which degrade catalog quality, customer experience, and seller competitiveness. Intended users include internal catalog management and search teams. The proposed solution employs deep learning to generate joint image and text embeddings from product images and titles, enabling the quantification of human-perceived similarity via numerical vectors. These embeddings are indexed and searched efficiently at scale using FAISS, overcoming quadratic matching complexity by converting item matching into a nearest-neighbor search problem. Compared against a traditional Elasticsearch baseline vector space model, the embedding approach demonstrated significantly higher recall, with complementary strengths between image- and text-based embeddings enhancing true duplicate detection. The system architecture supports indexing, search, and monitoring pipelines with low latency at high throughput, facilitating improved catalog deduplication and query analysis, with plans to extend to fashion item similarity and pricing comparisons.

Netflix addressed the business problem of enhancing streaming video quality for its viewers by replacing traditional video downscaling methods with a neural network-based "deep downscaler" integrated into their encoding pipeline. Intended for millions of Netflix members across devices, this solution employs a neural network architecture optimized to perform video downscaling that better preserves detail and sharpness before encoding with standard codecs like VP9 or AV1. The approach uses a preprocessing and resizing block trained to minimize mean squared error after upscaling, without requiring changes to client devices or encoding standards, thus ensuring broad compatibility and scalability on Netflix’s Cosmos encoding platform leveraging multi-CPU/GPU infrastructure. Evaluation via objective metrics (e.g., VMAF gains of 4.4–5.4%), subjective user preference (~77% favorability), and A/B streaming tests confirmed significant quality-of-experience improvements without playback issues. Efficiency considerations led to a lightweight network model focusing on luma filtering and integration within FFmpeg pipelines, balancing computational cost and visual gains. The deep downscaler marks a pragmatic step toward applying neural networks at scale across Netflix’s media encoding processes, with ongoing exploration for further neural network applications such as video denoising and codec innovations.

Spotify faced the business challenge of accurately forecasting user growth metrics across over 180 global markets, critical for performance monitoring and decision-making. Intended users include data scientists and business stakeholders requiring both automated and on-demand forecasts with actionable insights. The proposed solution is a scalable infrastructure segregating forecasts into mature markets (with extensive historical data for time series modeling and hyperparameter tuning), new markets (with limited data, addressed via proxy-based clustering models leveraging external macroeconomic and music data), and custom models requiring human input for nuanced cases like campaign-driven markets. Key components include a parameter-space creator, data labeler, hyperparameter tuner, model selector, and tools for QC, manual interventions, and visualization, all implemented using Google-managed Dataflow, BigQuery, and Kubernetes. Constraints include balancing fast iteration versus strict quality control, computational cost versus model complexity, and simplicity against accuracy gains. The outcome is a robust system enabling faster hyperparameter tuning and forecast delivery, enhanced model accuracy, integrated business input, and widespread internal visibility through automated visualizations and alerts.

Digits addresses the business problem of extracting valuable, structured information from unstructured banking transaction descriptions in real-time to better understand customers’ financial activities. Intended users include Digits’ customers who benefit from enhanced, human-readable transaction insights via Digits Search. The proposed solution leverages in-house Named Entity Recognition (NER) models built on state-of-the-art Transformer architectures, specifically fine-tuned BERT models implemented with TensorFlow 2.x and TensorFlow Text, allowing precise classification of tokens into entities like locations, URLs, and party names. Since no public datasets existed, annotations were manually created using the doccano tool, ensuring high-quality training data. The ML pipeline incorporates TensorFlow Extended (TFX) for production-ready training and Google Cloud’s Vertex AI for scalable deployment, with models served via TensorFlow Serving inside Kubernetes for low-latency, high-throughput inference. The outcome is an optimized, automated, and version-controlled system that delivers accurate, real-time semantic retrieval of transaction data, with a user-centric design that balances latency and accuracy, supports model rollbacks, and empowers customers to override entity predictions, thereby enhancing trust and usability.

Stitch Fix addresses the challenge of curating a large, diverse fashion inventory to match a growing client base by developing Style Explorer, an advanced merchandise recommender system that predicts item performance across client segments using over 500 features derived from human metadata, image embeddings, and client-item interactions. Targeting buyers and designers, Style Explorer integrates data from multiple sources and employs dimensionality reduction (UMAP) to manage sparse feature spaces before model training. Its performance is evaluated through business-centric simulation of buying decisions, comparing predicted vs. perfect model outcomes to prioritize areas for improvement. The system supports augmented inventory curation, AI-assisted design to reduce development cycles and waste, and strategic vendor portfolio analysis, including empowering BIPOC-owned brands via the Elevate program. By functioning as a core capability across supply chain functions, Style Explorer enhances personalization at scale, promotes sustainable purchasing, informs vendor onboarding, and aligns investments with client preferences to expansively and equitably grow Stitch Fix’s market presence.

The business problem addressed is the difficulty and privacy concerns of correcting grammatical errors on mobile devices, particularly during real-time text input on small smartphone screens like Pixel 6. Intended users include smartphone typists who need quick, on-the-fly grammar correction without transmitting data to external servers. The proposed solution is an on-device grammar correction system integrated into Gboard that employs a compact sequence-to-sequence neural network combining a Transformer encoder and LSTM decoder, trained via a novel hard distillation approach where a large cloud-based grammar model generates corrected sentence pairs and sentence prefixes to create a small, efficient 20MB model capable of low-latency inference within 22ms. Important data considerations include handling partial sentence inputs by determining grammatical correctness through heuristics that evaluate whether a prefix can complete a correct sentence, and transforming model outputs into user-friendly correction suggestions via Levenshtein distance alignment. The expected outcome is a privacy-preserving, real-time grammatical error correction feature that enhances typing accuracy and user experience across almost all apps using Gboard on Pixel 6 without reliance on cloud processing.

PayPal addresses the challenge of improving payment authorization rates by deploying machine learning models to predict issuer declines during card transactions, which occur due to factors like insufficient funds, stolen cards, or issuer-specific risk assessments. Intended for payment product teams and merchants, the solution aggregates historical transaction data at the card level—such as issuer decline ratios, card type, merchant industry, transaction timing, and approval history—and employs Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM) as the preferred tree-based algorithm optimized via Grid Search to handle inherently imbalanced classification data. Models predict specific decline types and facilitate proactive interventions, such as suggesting alternative payment methods or additional authentication, thereby enhancing approval accuracy beyond rule-based systems. This approach not only increases authorization rates but also supports transaction approvals during merchant outages or issuer declines for loyal customers, ultimately improving user experience and generating significant revenue uplift for online merchants.

Grammarly addresses the business problem of grammatical error correction (GEC) to improve written communication for users ranging from social media posters to job applicants by developing an AI-powered writing assistant. Traditional GEC approaches use neural machine translation models that translate erroneous sentences into corrected versions but often produce grammatically correct yet semantically inconsistent text. Grammarly’s proposed solution employs a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework, where a sequence-to-sequence generator produces corrected sentences and a sentence-pair discriminator evaluates the appropriateness of corrections relative to the input sentence, providing a context-aware reward signal. This adversarial training optimizes output quality beyond conventional n-gram metrics, tackling issues like semantic deviation and inappropriate edits. Experiments with RNN and transformer generators showed improved performance on standard GEC datasets, with the discriminator’s dual objective—to assess grammatical correctness and input-output alignment—being critical to success. This use of adversarial models tailored for GEC advances state-of-the-art correction quality by jointly optimizing linguistic validity and semantic coherence.

Grammarly’s ML and NLP teams addressed the challenge of understanding which parts of an email readers focus on to help users ensure their key messages are noticed. Aiming to model reader attention—a behavior difficult to label directly—they redefined attention as information retention and approximated it through reading speed measured at the sentence level. Because conventional eye-tracking methods were impractical at scale, they designed a novel, scalable interface showing one sentence at a time while blurring the rest, allowing precise timing of sentence reading without intrusive observation. Participants, tasked with summarizing each email’s intent to simulate typical reading goals, generated rich datasets normalized across readers. Using this data and guided by explainability constraints, they developed an interpretable cost-value model leveraging linguistic features to predict attention heatmaps, outperforming traditional heuristics by reducing prediction errors and increasing recall. Their iterative approach integrates computational linguistics expertise and extensive feature engineering to refine predictions, with ongoing work to capture diverse reading behaviors and contexts for improved semantic retrieval of reader attention in email communication.

Brex addressed the business problem of opaque and inaccurate credit card merchant descriptors, which hindered businesses’ ability to track expenses and close books efficiently, by developing an automated system called Auto Merchant Cat. Targeted at financial operations teams within growing companies using corporate cards, this solution combines semantic retrieval via Google Places API for merchant identification—cleansing raw descriptors to retrieve DBA names and websites—and machine learning classifiers that leverage features such as inferred sentence embeddings of merchant names, Merchant Category Codes (MCC), and Google Place Types to categorize merchants into one of 48 predefined business accounting categories. When automated components fail, the system escalates to crowdsourced human workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk with stringent quality controls, and unresolved cases proceed to manual support, ensuring high accuracy. The pipeline, orchestrated by Airflow, retrains models monthly with updated labeled data, sustaining classification precision above 75% and keeping error rates below 5%, thereby enabling scalable, robust expense categorization critical for corporate financial management.

Pinterest addresses the challenge of maintaining a positive and safe comment ecosystem amid increasing native content from creators by deploying a scalable, near-real-time multi-task machine learning model. Intended for trust and safety engineers and content moderators, the solution uses a fine-tuned multilingual DistilBERT transformer combined with contextual features from Pins, Pinners, and comments to classify comments into facets such as unsafe, spam, sentiment (positive, neutral, negative), and quality (based on readability, relevance, and nuance). Training relied on a cost-effective human-verified dataset primarily for English, augmented with sentiment analysis tools and quality annotations. The model is deployed via a streaming data platform integrating Kafka and Flink for real-time inference and serves two workflows: filtering harmful content and ranking comments by quality to surface constructive interactions. This approach led to a 53% decrease in comment report rates, fostering a healthier community experience and enabling future extensions to other text-based interactions like messaging and captioning.

Mercado Libre addresses forecasting challenges in their marketplace by developing global time series (GTS) models to predict both sales—actual transactions constrained by stock—and demand—the potential sales if stock were unlimited—for individual items sold by first-party sellers across countries. Their solution employs Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks capable of multi-step forecasting, leveraging cleaned, log-transformed sales data and features such as past visits, product questions, price variations, and stock levels, adapting dynamically to diverse item behaviors including intermittent sales. By distinguishing sales from demand using stock availability, two specialized models were trained with distinct objectives and evaluated primarily via Mean Absolute Error (MAE). The sales forecast accurately tracks declining sales due to stock depletion, while the demand model anticipates sales recovery when stock is replenished. Incorporating event-driven adjustments as post-processing, the approach enables more informed inventory restocking decisions despite noisy, short, and heterogeneous time series data. Future enhancements aim to capture forecast uncertainty through probabilistic methods to further optimize replenishment strategies for internal stakeholders and ultimately improve marketplace performance.

Stitch Fix addresses the challenge of delivering contextually relevant, query-based personalized recommendations to enhance client shopping experiences by integrating multiple latent representation spaces and personalization models. Their users are online shoppers inspired by community-shared images ("community inspiration") depicting styled outfits, which serve as queries. The solution employs computer vision to detect clothing items within these images and maps them to "anchor items" in Stitch Fix’s catalog, representing them as sets of latent style embeddings in a shared client-item space. Recommendations are generated by scoring the similarity of these embeddings to the client's preferences, selecting exemplar images accordingly, then leveraging a hybrid similarity space combining visual and client-response features to identify product neighbors. A multi-objective ranking balances the relevance to the inspirational image (via distance in embedding space) and predicted client affinity, with diversity enforced across item categories. This approach unifies multiple domain-specific latent spaces—style, client preference, and visual similarity—and models owned by specialized teams, enabling Stitch Fix to provide personalized, context-sensitive recommendations that mirror both client tastes and current trends, optimizing engagement and purchase likelihood.

DoorDash addresses the complex dispatch problem—optimally matching orders, merchants, and Dashers to maximize delivery efficiency and customer satisfaction—using a sophisticated system called DeepRed that combines machine learning and mixed-integer optimization. Intended for marketplace operators managing millions of daily deliveries, the solution predicts order prep times, travel times, and Dasher acceptance probabilities through ML models, which feed into an optimization layer that scores, batches, and dispatches orders dynamically considering factors like geographic proximity, batching opportunities, supply-demand balance, and real-world constraints such as traffic and weather. To handle challenges like model drift, overfitting, and variability accumulation, DeepRed employs continuous model retraining, Bayesian optimization for parameter tuning, and variance-aware scoring. The system's effectiveness is continuously enhanced through extensive simulations that mimic diverse market conditions and rigorous experimentation using advanced statistical designs to validate impacts on key business metrics, supported by a multidisciplinary data science team combining expertise in optimization, causal inference, and ML within gig economy and rideshare contexts.

Financial institutions face the challenge of detecting money laundering, a complex and evolving financial crime linked to global criminal activity and terrorism financing. Traditional rule-based Anti-Money Laundering (AML) systems generate numerous binary alerts that are difficult to prioritize and adapt to changing behaviors. Capital One developed a machine learning-driven suspicious activity monitoring system, powered by a scalable random forest model trained on extensive historical investigations and hundreds of transaction and customer features to score alerts by risk level. This model enhances alert prioritization, enabling AML investigators to focus on high-risk activities and reduce false positives, thereby improving investigation efficiency. Developed through close collaboration between machine learning experts and AML professionals with domain-specific insights across multiple countries, the system supports transparency, explainability, and regulatory compliance. Continuous monitoring and feature optimization maintain model accuracy and adaptability amid evolving customer behaviors, ultimately enabling more effective detection and mitigation of money laundering activities.

Twitter's Interactive Query team addresses scalability and performance challenges in processing petabyte-scale SQL data across federated on-premises and cloud clusters by forecasting SQL query resource usage using machine learning. Intended for data analysts, DevOps, and system schedulers, the solution trains two classification models using historical SQL query request logs, vectorized via NLP techniques like bag-of-words and TF-IDF, to predict CPU time and peak memory consumption without relying on traditional query plans or SQL engine statistics. By discretizing continuous resource metrics into categorical classes aligned with operational thresholds (e.g., CPU time under 30 seconds as lightweight), and employing XGBoost classifiers, the system achieves over 97% accuracy, with robust precision and recall especially for high-resource queries. The trained models are deployed as scalable RESTful APIs within Twitter’s Mesos-managed Aurora containers to provide near real-time (approx. 200 ms) predictions that support query scheduling, preemptive scaling, and BI tool resource estimations, thereby enhancing productivity and infrastructure efficiency in large-scale analytics environments.

This use case addresses the challenge faced by delivery drivers in precisely locating customer doorsteps when GPS data is noisy or incomplete due to obscured house numbers and urban canyon effects. Intended for logistics teams and delivery apps, the solution leverages a learning-to-rank machine learning approach that predicts the most accurate doorstep coordinates from historical GPS delivery data. By framing location prediction as a ranking problem over candidate points—derived from clustering GPS data and nearby building geometries—and training a random forest model on pairwise comparisons with features such as GPS density and proximity to streets or buildings, the method outperforms baseline centroid and kernel density estimation techniques. Constraints include variability in map completeness and limited candidate sets per address, but the offline computation allows thorough pairwise comparisons at inference. The expected outcome is significantly improved accuracy in pinpointing delivery drop-off locations, enhancing efficiency for Amazon Last Mile drivers and customer satisfaction.

The business challenge addressed is the increasing cost and complexity of online payment fraud in ecommerce, impacting merchants through direct losses, chargeback fees, and customer attrition. Intended users are businesses processing payments who need to balance fraud prevention with minimizing false declines of legitimate transactions. The solution, Stripe Radar, leverages adaptive machine learning trained on vast transactional data from the Stripe network to predict fraud likelihood in real-time, utilizing hundreds of engineered features—including novel embeddings of categorical variables—to detect nuanced fraud patterns and adapt rapidly to evolving threats. Constraints include the tradeoff between false negatives (fraud missed) and false positives (legitimate transactions blocked), model deployment challenges such as real-time feature computation and model drift, and the need to integrate seamlessly with existing payment flows without engineering overhead. Expected outcomes are reduced fraudulent transactions, optimized block rates aligned to business margins, minimized customer friction, and continuous model improvements through automated monitoring and evaluation pipelines, supplemented by customizable rules and manual reviews for business-specific fraud patterns.

Retailers on the Ocado Smart Platform (OSP) face the challenge of balancing stock availability with minimizing waste (purge) amid fluctuating grocery ecommerce demand influenced by freshness constraints and shifting customer behavior. To support demand planners, Ocado’s Supply Chain and Data Science team developed a suite of machine learning models—from heuristic algorithms for new retailers lacking sufficient data, to feed-forward neural networks that optimize heuristic combinations per product, and advanced deep sequence-to-sequence neural networks that mimic human forecasting by memorizing long-term demand patterns and generalizing across products and promotions. These models leverage recent sales data and adapt to external factors like promotions and global events for millions of daily forecasts at Customer Fulfilment Centre scale. Future efforts include building generalized neural networks for quick deployment with new retailers, fine-tuning to specific trends, and modeling forecast uncertainty to inform better stock decisions, ultimately enhancing availability and profitability for diverse retailer business models across varying markets and geographies.

This use case addresses the challenge of engaging app users with push notifications without causing spam or channel saturation, targeting customers of Mercado Pago QR-enabled stores who often receive excessive and unrelated communications. The intended users are mobile app customers and sellers within the Mercado Libre ecosystem. The solution employs a scalable, modular machine learning-driven orchestration process using Python on the Fury Data Apps platform to dynamically select and score candidate user-store notification pairs across multiple marketing strategies (e.g., market basket analysis identifying purchase affinities between Merchant Category Codes and ON to OFF bridging online interest with nearby physical stores), deduplicating and prioritizing them for push delivery at optimal times. Key data includes user behavior, purchase patterns, geolocation, and store categories, with constraints like avoiding repeated or irrelevant notifications to prevent user fatigue. The expected outcome is increased engagement measured by higher open rates (in some cases doubling previous metrics), ensuring personalized, timely, and relevant notifications that enhance user experience and seller acceptance while preventing exhaustion of communication channels.

Dropbox faced the business challenge of involuntary churn and disrupted revenue flow caused by payment failures during subscription renewals, impacting customer satisfaction and retention. Their intended users are paying customers with subscriptions prone to renewal failures due to issues like insufficient funds or expired cards. The proposed solution applies machine learning models—specifically a gradient boosted ranking model—to predict the optimal timing for retrying failed payment charges within a renewal window, replacing static, manually maintained rule-based billing policies. The system integrates payment and customer usage data, serves predictions through a low-latency ML platform, and continuously monitors business and model metrics for reliability and performance. Expected outcomes include higher payment success rates, reduced collection times, improved customer experience, and streamlined operations by eliminating complex manual interventions, with ongoing A/B testing validating ML-driven improvements globally.

Apple addresses the challenge of optimizing user experiences while preserving privacy by developing interpretable, adaptive statistical learning algorithms for sequential hypothesis testing and reinforcement learning under delayed, noisy, and differentially private feedback. Their solution combines empirical Bayesian shrinkage estimation and Thompson sampling bandits, applied notably in App Store product page optimization to identify the most engaging variants (e.g., app icons) that drive downloads. This approach manages delays and noise by smoothing estimates over time, enhancing stability and interpretability for human operators who balance learning yield and decision-making. By enabling robust, privacy-aware reward estimation and sequential hypothesis testing with Bayes factors, the system minimizes false positives and adapts smoothly even amid non-stationary user responses, facilitating trustworthy, data-driven improvements and developer insights in a complex, privacy-constrained environment.

DoorDash addresses the challenge of managing vast volumes of image data collected by delivery drivers to automate verification tasks such as checking pizza bag equipment, store closures, and catering setups, where manual review is impractical. Targeted at internal business teams, the solution replaces costly and slow third-party vendors with an in-house, scalable image recognition pipeline using transfer learning on pre-trained ResNet models fine-tuned with limited labeled data, integrated via daily ETL or real-time services. The lightweight system enables rapid iteration, fast deployment, privacy-compliant data handling, and continuous performance monitoring, prioritizing use cases based on business impact, feasibility with image classification, and availability of annotated data. This reusable approach accelerates onboarding of new image recognition applications, improves cost efficiency, and supports diverse logistics and fraud detection needs at scale across DoorDash’s growing operations.

Gousto addresses personalized meal kit recommendations through its Rouxcommender family, tailored to different customer journeys and preferences. The business challenge is to present weekly menus that cater not only to the majority preference (meat eaters) but also to niche dietary needs like vegetarian or vegan customers, ensuring inclusivity and improved customer satisfaction. Intended users include potential customers ("Gousto Recommends"), new customers ("Rouxcommender Junior"), and long-term customers ("Rouxcommender Senior"). The solution involves layered recommenders: initially showcasing popular recipes with emerging adjustments for dietary diversity, then leveraging first-box order data to recommend similar or explorative recipes to recent joiners via similarity measures in attributes or co-order patterns, and finally applying a dual-tower neural embedding model to capture detailed preferences for seasoned customers while overcoming the cold-start problem for new recipes. Data constraints feature highly dynamic menus and diverse customer tastes, with outcomes expected to enhance basket match rates and provide personalized, evolving recommendations that reflect individual and cluster taste profiles.

Nextdoor addresses the business problem of keeping neighbors informed with relevant, timely notifications about new or trending local posts that matter to them, enhancing community engagement and user retention. Intended users are Nextdoor neighbors who receive email, push, and in-product notifications customizable by frequency. The proposed solution employs machine learning, specifically an XGBoost model combining content-based, recipient-based, and author-based features—including embeddings for text similarity—to predict individual notification relevance and optimize click and tap rates. To manage user experience constraints, the system enforces personalized weekly notification budgets per channel, dynamically controlled via PID feedback loops that adjust relevance thresholds to respect these budgets in real time, balancing notification volume and quality. This approach has yielded significant improvements in engagement metrics and reduced unsubscribes, particularly by better targeting dormant users, while ongoing challenges include tuning thresholds for responsiveness and handling outages affecting model features. Nextdoor plans to evolve toward a hybrid system integrating scheduled and real-time notifications to improve robustness and further optimize delivery timing and relevance.

This use case addresses the business problem of improving customer support prioritization to reduce churn and enhance satisfaction, targeting customer support teams as intended users. The proposed solution is a supervised machine learning model that predicts support tickets at risk of low customer satisfaction by combining diverse inputs such as customer demographics, ticket attributes (severity, age, escalations), workload of support reps, and product information, using customer feedback from post-support surveys as labels despite known biases and response variability. The approach overcomes manual prioritization limitations by analyzing dozens of relevant case attributes simultaneously, enabling proactive focus on higher-risk cases. Model training involved careful validation to optimize for low false positives and achieved an 80% AUC, resulting in approximately a 10% improvement in customer satisfaction scores for tickets acted upon based on model predictions. Continuous model refinement incorporates stakeholder feedback and feature importance reviews to maintain prediction accuracy and align with evolving support dynamics.

This use case addresses the challenge of extracting actionable insights from large volumes of customer support cases to prioritize engineering investments and improve product experience. The intended users are product owners and feature teams who need to identify and address prevalent and emerging customer pain points revealed through support tickets. The proposed solution leverages semantic retrieval through natural language processing and topic modeling, initially employing Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) with text preprocessing to cluster cases by semantic similarity and reveal dominant issues, alongside trend analysis to track topic evolution over time. Recognizing limitations in capturing nuanced language, the approach evolves to use transfer-based models like DistilBERT for generating embeddings that reflect semantic context more effectively, followed by dimensionality reduction with UMAP and clustering with HDBSCAN to handle noise and outliers while discovering dense clusters without requiring preset cluster counts. Class-based TF-IDF is applied for coherent topic representation. This enables proactive prioritization of support issues by product teams, efficient resource alignment, tracking of intervention effectiveness, and ultimately, the reduction of support demands by addressing root causes. Constraints include the need for careful text cleaning and hyperparameter tuning in traditional methods, while transformer-based models reduce these burdens at the cost of computational complexity. The expected outcome is improved customer satisfaction through targeted product improvements driven by scalable, semantically informed analysis of support data.

Scribd faces the challenge of classifying a diverse, large corpus of user-uploaded documents—ranging from text-heavy reports to comics and sheet music—without relying on language or content specifics, to enhance content discovery and recommendation systems. To address this, their Applied Research team developed a multi-component machine learning solution leveraging semantic understanding and user behavior, starting with a computer vision-based page classification model trained via active learning on carefully hand-labeled pages across six document types plus an "other" category to manage out-of-distribution inputs. Using a lightweight architecture (SqueezeNet) optimized for efficient inference at scale, they classify sampled pages and ensemble predictions with document metadata for robust, language-agnostic document-level classification, overcoming challenges like mislabeled heterogeneous pages and overconfident wrong predictions through adversarial retraining and specialized binary classifiers. This foundational semantic retrieval enables tailored information extraction pipelines per document type, advancing Scribd’s ability to automatically interpret and organize their extensive document library.

Scribd’s Applied Research team addressed the challenge of extracting meaningful metadata from text-heavy user-uploaded documents to enhance their discovery and recommendation systems by developing a multi-component machine learning pipeline for semantic information extraction. The intended users are discovery and content recommendation systems that benefit from enriched document representations. The solution involves unsupervised keyphrase extraction based on n-grams and language-specific rules to identify major themes, combined with named entity recognition and normalization techniques to unify aliases referencing the same unique entity, facilitated by heuristics and entity linking to a knowledge base (e.g., Wikidata) to disambiguate entities and enrich document semantics. The approach accounts for alias ambiguity by linking mentions contextually or fallback heuristic methods, enabling uniform document representation through embeddings of linked keyphrases and entities. This yields improved document understanding, thematic clustering, and analogical discovery within a shared embedding space, ultimately enhancing content organization and recommendation outcomes.

Capital One addresses the business problem of minimizing customer impact from complex, interconnected application failures in their digital banking services by automating incident management through machine learning. Intended for engineering and DevOps teams, the solution integrates large-scale, real-time streaming data from diverse monitoring tools across APIs, microservices, databases, and infrastructure layers, overcoming data silos and complexity to detect anomalous patterns. A unique combination of specialized time-series anomaly detection models and a Bayesian Network-based causal inference engine identifies the root cause component among many potentially failing nodes in interconnected systems, enabling precise and rapid diagnosis. Alerts enriched with an intuitive UI are seamlessly integrated into existing workflows, reducing dependency on specialized engineers and accelerating time-to-resolution by up to 50%, thereby decreasing downtime and preserving customer trust in 24/7 digital banking. Future enhancements aim to extend from detection to preventive measures and automated remediation recommendations.

Wayfair's business problem involves optimizing ad spend across millions of SKUs and keywords in auction-based advertising channels to ensure effective bid placement that balances cost and return on investment (ROI). The intended users include marketing analysts, data scientists, and algorithm developers who require a scalable, extensible platform enabling fine-grained control, experimentation, and observability of bidding strategies. The proposed solution is a centralized, modular Ads Bidding Platform featuring reusable Single Bid Calculators (SBCs) that incorporate rule-based and machine learning approaches, an arbitration mechanism to select optimal bids from multiple models, and a data engineering pipeline (FORGE) to process diverse first- and third-party signals. Key constraints include the need for scalability across millions of items, low-latency data retrieval via Aerospike, and adaptability to different advertising vendors through vendor mapping. The expected outcome is a data-driven, intelligent bidding system that improves ad placement efficiency, reduces redundant development effort, enhances transparency, and accelerates innovation in bidding algorithms while supporting expansion to additional marketing channels.

PayPal addresses the complex and evolving problem of payment fraud detection in its global e-commerce network by leveraging a proprietary real-time graph database and graph analysis platform tailored to model buyer-seller transaction relationships as vertices and edges. Intended for risk analysts, data scientists, and fraud prevention teams, this solution integrates sub-second latency graph queries using Gremlin DSL and near real-time event-based updates to identify fraud patterns, such as account takeovers and coordinated fraud rings, by analyzing discrete and connected graph properties. The platform incorporates scalable, fault-tolerant infrastructure with offline and streaming data ingestion, graph visualization tools for interactive investigations, and machine learning techniques including graph embeddings to predict fraudulent behaviors at node, edge, and graph levels despite concept drift in fraud tactics. The expected outcome is enhanced real-time detection of repeat and organized fraudsters, facilitating proactive mitigation that significantly reduces financial risk while supporting compliance with data privacy requirements.

Wayfair addresses the challenge of accurately describing product colors in natural language, crucial for enhancing customer shopping by improving color filtering and product discovery. Their intended users are Wayfair customers who filter products by color and internal teams managing product data. The solution involves developing an algorithmic color taxonomy that hierarchically organizes RGB values into multiple granular levels using delta-E color difference metrics, clustering techniques like K-means and Birch, and graph-based methods to relate closely associated colors. This taxonomy maps RGBs extracted from product images—bounded by human annotators—to descriptive color names spanning from highly granular shades to basic color categories. Color tagging employs dominant color extraction via clustering and fast nearest neighbor search with faiss for efficient mapping. Evaluation combines supplier tags and human judgment, achieving an 88% acceptance rate, while ongoing work aims to improve robustness against image noise and incorporate metallic finish detection using convolutional neural networks. This approach enhances the precision, completeness, and granularity of product color metadata to improve search relevance and customer experience on Wayfair’s platform.

Shopify addresses the challenge of categorizing and enriching product data at massive scale for millions of merchants, each with unique business goals, by deploying fine-tuned multimodal Qwen models that analyze rich image and text inputs to classify products and generate detailed metadata, enabling hundreds of millions of inferences daily. This semantic retrieval solution underpins broader commerce optimizations including fraud detection, personalized merchant assistance via LLaMa-based models, product discovery through Nomic embeddings, and accurate financial forecasting with tabular transformer models, all powered by advanced GPU infrastructure and continuous access to frontier AI models to handle high-throughput, low-latency demands. The intended users are Shopify merchants seeking improved product presentation, discovery, and business operations, while the expected outcome is more effective, customized merchant support leading to increased success across Shopify’s complex, evolving marketplace.

Dailymotion addresses the business problem of improving contextual advertising by enhancing video content categorization at scale while maintaining user privacy amid declining cookie usage. The intended users include advertisers and platform partners who currently classify videos using broad categories. The solution employs deep learning with computer vision, specifically a multi-label video classification model based on the NeXtVLAD architecture, trained end-to-end with video frame features from InceptionV3 and enriched with in-house metadata. The model predicts fine-grained, visually discernible IAB taxonomy categories (196 selected), complementing existing textual models to boost classification coverage and granularity, especially for non-textual or multilingual content. The system uses predicted labels from textual models as noisy ground truth for visual model training due to limited labeled data. Constraints include focusing on visually identifiable categories and short videos (1–10 minutes) for effective frame-based classification. The production pipeline scales frame extraction and inference to process millions of videos using Klio. This approach achieves up to 64% coverage at 80% precision, significantly enhancing the number and accuracy of IAB category predictions per video, thereby enriching contextual ad targeting and user experience without compromising privacy.

Facebook addresses the challenge of personalizing News Feed ranking for over 2 billion users with diverse interests and vast content by employing advanced machine learning techniques such as multitask neural networks, embeddings, and offline learning systems to predict the relevance of posts to each user. The system optimizes a complex objective function aggregating multiple engagement signals (likes, comments, shares) weighted according to surveys reflecting users’ perceptions of meaningful interactions, handling thousands of features per user-post pair in real time. This scalable ranking pipeline queries candidate posts—including fresh, unseen, and conversation-boosted content—scores them with neural models, and merges predictions through a multi-pass architecture incorporating diversity and integrity rules, ultimately generating a personalized ranked feed. Users benefit from seeing content that aligns closely with their interests and engagement habits, enhancing long-term value and social connection on a global scale.

DoorDash addresses the complex business problem of balancing the supply of delivery drivers ("Dashers") with consumer order demand to ensure timely deliveries, consistent pricing, and positive experiences for consumers, Dashers, and merchants. The intended users include Dashers, consumers, merchants, and internal operations teams. Their solution leverages machine learning, specifically a multivariate regression forecasting model using LightGBM, to generate high-fidelity supply and demand predictions at localized market-time units. These forecasts feed into a mixed-integer programming optimizer that allocates targeted incentives to mobilize Dashers while respecting budgetary and regional constraints, considering uncertainty through resampling techniques to manage supply-demand variances effectively. Key data considerations include ensuring that forecasting granularity matches decision-making units, incorporating relevant covariates to avoid spurious correlations, and simplifying data dependencies to boost model reliability and maintainability amid rapid organizational growth. The expected outcomes include reduced delivery times and cancellations, improved order fulfillment, optimized incentive allocation that meets budgets, and enhanced system agility for continuous experimentation and scaling.

PayPal faces the business problem of combating sophisticated, evolving fraud and cybercrimes in real-time, requiring highly accurate and fair machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models subject to regulatory constraints. The intended users are data scientists and ML engineers developing and deploying fraud detection models. The proposed solution is the "Quokka" ML shadow platform, an end-to-end CI/CD framework that enables continuous integration, automated deployment, and real-time auditing of multiple model versions in a production-similar shadow environment where models can be safely tested without affecting live decisioning. The platform handles heterogeneous, temporal, and dynamic fraud data by supporting temporally aware features and iterative model retraining with recent data. Important constraints include strict real-time inferencing SLAs, data parity challenges between offline training and live production, and the need to avoid costly rollbacks. The platform integrates self-service UI/UX, automated pipelines, auditing compute clusters, and uses technologies like Hadoop, TensorFlow, and MLFlow to deliver rapid, maintainable, and scalable deployment. Expected outcomes include drastically reduced model development-to-release time by 80%, tripled productivity, zero production rollbacks, extended operational coverage from 8x5 to 24x7, and accelerating adoption of fraud models by teams quarter-over-quarter.

Google Photos addresses the business problem of users being overwhelmed by vast, disorganized digital photo libraries, which obscure meaningful moments that users intended to document and remember. The intended users are diverse consumers with varying photo habits, who seek an enjoyable and personalized reminiscing experience. The proposed AI-powered solution leverages semantic retrieval through machine learning models that identify and curate significant photos by filtering out duplicates, low-quality images, and irrelevant content using pixel-based aesthetic scoring and non-pixel-based detection for labels such as people, pets, and objects, combined with rule-based metadata filtering for screenshots and low-resolution images. Recognizing the personal and sensitive nature of reminiscing, the system incorporates user controls allowing individuals to exclude certain faces, dates, or entire memories, addressing the probabilistic limitations of AI and respecting emotional context. The expected outcome is an immersive, meaningful Memories feature that surfaces engaging, personalized photo content, facilitating everyday reminiscing while maintaining user trust through transparency and control mechanisms.

Scribd addresses the challenge of personalizing content recommendations for millions of users from a vast catalog—including premium ebooks and user-uploaded items—by shifting from collaborative filtering to Transformer-based sequential recommendation models that produce semantic embeddings of users and items. To serve low-latency, scalable recommendations with complex faceted filters (e.g., language, geography, content type), they built an embedding-based retrieval system atop Elasticsearch, which functions both as a key-value store for user embeddings and a vector similarity search engine with custom script scoring (dot product) and multi-search capabilities. Despite Elasticsearch's limitations such as lack of in-memory partial updates, it met requirements for facet filtering, update batching, availability, and latency (p95 <100ms). Data ingestion and model retraining are orchestrated via Apache Spark and Airflow with daily user embedding updates and weekly item embedding refreshes. Load testing confirmed system resilience at ~50 QPS, and A/B testing with over 1 million users demonstrated statistically significant improvements in engagement metrics, validating the approach's business impact on personalized content discovery.

Wayfair addresses the challenge of evolving customer preferences in furniture recommendations by deploying MARS, a transformer-based sequential recommender system tailored for capturing changes in taste over time from simple input sequences of browsed items. Designed for product categories with dynamic catalogs and interrelated styles across different furniture types, MARS leverages multi-headed self-attention and learned positional embeddings to model customers' recent browsing behavior, thereby enhancing relevance beyond static matrix factorization methods. The system processes cleaned sequences, removes infrequent or duplicate items, and outputs ranked recommendations using embeddings that encode item similarity and positional context, with regularization techniques preventing overfitting. Results demonstrate a 67% improvement in recall for substitutable product recommendations and reveal that learned embeddings capture transferable style preferences across complementary and co-viewed product categories, even when controlling for class effects. This approach enables more accurate, style-aware recommendations for customers with or without direct browsing history in a specific class, setting a foundation for future enhancements incorporating richer user and product data.

Walmart’s e-commerce platform addresses the business problem of poor product discoverability caused by incorrect or default product taxonomy hierarchies, which negatively impact SEO and shelving accuracy. Intended users are internal teams managing product catalogs and shelving. The solution applies deep learning, specifically a CNN-LSTM multi-class classification model trained on department-specific product data (product name, description, etc.) to predict accurate Product Type (PT) labels within a three-level taxonomy (Product Category, Product Family, Product Type). Constraints include handling large, multi-departmental product sets requiring pre-processing of textual attributes and ensuring model predictions meet a confidence threshold; predictions feed into automated shelving rules executed regularly via catalog APIs. Expected outcomes include improved accuracy (88% validation, 80% manual) in PT classification, enabling better shelving assignments and thus enhanced product visibility and SEO on Walmart.com.

Lifen addresses the challenge of accurately detecting varied and complex layouts in medical PDF documents from thousands of clients to transform a 2D grid of words into a coherent 1D sequence suitable for NLP models or plain text export, avoiding costly OCR when possible. The key users are NLP engineers and document processing teams requiring fast, precise, and customizable layout extraction.
